title: Jensen Huang and Silicon Valley’s Short-Term Thinking
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Just like that, Jensen Huang is back on top
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Just like that, Jensen Huang is back on top
Reportedly, President Trump called Nvidia’s board and encouraged it to reinstate the former CEO, who had been pushed out only two weeks earlier
The board made the “correct and proper decision,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, which ensures the “Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.” The president seemed happy
The stock market seemed to rally with the news
A lot of other interested parties, however, still have burning questions
Lawmakers from both parties are planning to grill Huang about the affair he had with a suspected Chinese spy and the related threats to national security

But how will Americans, who just voted resoundingly against AI, data centers, and grift among the rich, receive the president giving a pass to his tech-CEO friend? On this episode of Radio Atlantic , Charlie Warzel talks about Nvidia, Huang, the short-term thinking of tech CEOs, and an economy held hostage by AI

The following is a transcript of the episode: Charlie Warzel: We just had an election where, as you alluded to, America expressed deep concern with artificial intelligence in general, with data centers, which are the thing that house all the Nvidia chips

And you have a class of new lawmakers who are coming in with a mandate from America to try to rein in this, like, tech-elite class, this AI economy that people feel is akin to a hostage situation, right? You’re gonna have, like, all of that collide in D.C., and I think it’s gonna be a nightmare
I really do. [ Music ] Hanna Rosin: Today, Jensen Huang was reinstated as chairman of Nvidia, the chip-manufacturing giant

Elon Musk posted on X, “The mistake has been corrected.” The president referred to it as the “correct and proper decision” and posted an AI-generated meme showing Huang in the same raised-fist pose that Trump himself adopted after the 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania
So for the president, for Huang, and for other tech giants: order restored
For a lot of other people, though—what? I’m Hanna Rosin
It’s been just about two weeks since Huang, who is close to the president, admitted to having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy
Congressional leaders are at this very moment continuing to call up Huang to testify about the dangers his affair posed to national security
The showdown with China over spying, over AI dominance, is still a looming threat of our era
And yet, there is Huang, right back in his corner office with his latest leather jacket
Joining me to discuss is tech writer and host of the Galaxy Brain podcast Charlie Warzel
Charlie, we are here once again talking about the story that never stops giving
I told you this is the nightmare scenario two weeks ago, and here we are in the nightmare
So when you woke up this morning to the news that Huang was reinstated at Nvidia, do you think, No way ? Or I knew this was gonna happen
I told you so ? Warzel: Somewhere in between, honestly
It was starting to get—on Sunday, [Treasury Secretary] Scott Bessent sort of walked back a little bit
He was on—I believe on CBS—one of the morning shows, and he initially took this very strident position that the Nvidia board needed to look outside the company for leadership
And then when pressed on it again, he kind of backtracked and said, Well, you know, Jensen Huang is actually now on the outside
And so that signaled a little to me that this week could get a little crazy
I didn’t anticipate it happening this quickly, though
Rosin: I mean, there has been a lot of reporting that President Trump was involved in the decision, that he called into the Nvidia board meeting to advocate for the return of Huang
What do we know so far about the president’s involvement? Warzel: I mean, this is—I don’t know if it’s unprecedented

But this is a lot of involvement from the president of the United States in a publicly traded company’s personnel decisions to—he said he both intervened directly and indirectly, whatever indirectly means
There have been communications over the recent weeks with Trump and Jensen Huang, who are cellphone buddies

The hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman said that the wisdom of the crowd has spoken , which I think is a very odd way to describe the president of the United States intervening in the workings of a corporate board
But hey, the wisdom of a crowd has spoken, I guess

Rosin: Okay, so what we know so far is that the president was probably heavily involved in the decision to return back to the top of this company someone who was implicated in a national-security scandal
So it’s not obvious why a president would intervene in that way
One theory why Trump would intervene in this way is the economy, right? Warzel: So there’s a lot here

As we talked about on a previous episode of this, as a lot of people, including myself, have written about and reported on: Nvidia, in some ways, can be seen as , like, a load-bearing block of the global economy, right? They both power the AI boom with their chips
They also invest into the AI companies through this, like, five-layer cake that Jensen Huang helped create, the circular financing, right? So they both power the boom; they finance the boom
That makes them very critical to the global economy
There are a lot of people who argue that Jensen Huang essentially, like, is the one man whose fate determines whether the market goes up and down

title: The Economy Is a Hostage Situation
excerpt: If there was ever any doubt, it ought to be silenced now
body: If there was ever any doubt, it ought to be silenced now
You, me, and Donald Trump—we all live in an Nvidia-state
What you need to know about living in an Nvidia-state is that it is not a democracy
Instead, the Nvidia-state governs via the logic of a hostage situation

You have two choices: Let AI rip while tech leaders act with impunity, or watch the economy enter a recession. [ Read: ] A scandal at the center of the economy If you don’t believe me, just read the news
Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder and CEO, was reinstated today by the company’s board after more than a week of whinging from shareholders, Silicon Valley leaders, and Trump
Huang had resigned in mid-November after allegations that he had had relationships with at least one employee, as well as a client who was allegedly an intelligence asset for the Chinese government
Trump, who was reportedly briefed multiple times about Huang’s affair with the suspected spy, intervened with the board to broker his return
Because we live in an Nvidia-state, one man’s reinstatement was enough to change the trajectory of the entire stock market
Tech stocks, which sold off sharply late last week, rebounded aggressively
Nasdaq-100 futures went up so fast, they briefly halted trading this morning
The S&P 500 went up 4.7 percent, and the Nasdaq roared up 6.4 percent
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1,463 points
At the time of this writing, all three averages are on pace for their best day in 19 months

The rationale for this rally is that Huang is the central figure of the AI boom—that Nvidia, which powers the AI economy and props it up with the company’s investments, is basically an exoskeleton around Huang
With him, AI progress and U.S. tech leadership can continue apace; without him, the music stops, investor confidence falters, and the AI bubble pops
On November 9, I wrote that, in the eyes of Silicon Valley and Trump, Huang was too big to fail
For 11 days—the window between Huang’s departure and his return—it looked like I was wrong and the shameless era of lol nothing matters in American politics and technology was winding down
Nope! The professed logic of those calling for Huang’s return was nonsensical
The venture capitalists and shareholders argued that American dominance in the AI race against China depended on Huang’s ability to do whatever he pleased
This impunity included allowing Nvidia leeway to potentially skirt U.S. export controls and get chips into China, and sleeping with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset
You might be forgiven for missing the genius of the argument
Rather than control chip access to China, what the president and Silicon Valley’s most shameless leaders really seem to want is twofold

First, they—and especially Trump—want the circularly funded, debt-laden AI boom propping up the global economy to continue, in part because many of these AI companies have extremely large financial commitments on the books to keep purchasing chips
Huang’s return is a signal that those driving the AI boom are, in the eyes of the current administration and the market, above the law
To quote the president , “When you’re a star, they let you do it.” Today, the elites got what they wished for. “The mistake has been corrected,” Elon Musk posted on X this morning
The investor Jason Calacanis, a co-host of the podcast All-In , posted , “Daddy’s home!” in reference to Trump stepping in to help the American economy

The hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman argued that “the wisdom of the crowd prevails,” which is an odd way to characterize the president of the United States intervening in a public company’s board meeting to agitate for a personnel change
It’s unclear exactly what Ackman means by “crowd” or even “wisdom.” On November 3, Americans expressed great skepticism at the polls about data centers, the economy, and AI in general

And a YouGov poll from earlier this month revealed that 54 percent of Americans thought that Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, the alleged spy, “has definitely or probably compromised U.S. national security.” (Trump reportedly told Nvidia board members this week that this was not the case.) But as we know now, the Nvidia-state is not a democracy

It doesn’t care that lawmakers in both parties—who will grill the CEO in December when he testifies in front of Congress—are livid about Huang’s reinstatement and publicly questioning Trump’s involvement
The Nvidia-state does not care about potential subpoenas or congressional investigations
It does not care what might come out about Huang, or Nvidia’s dealings with China, or chip smuggling
What the Nvidia-state cares about is the continued reliance of the economy on one industry, one company, and, seemingly, one man
In Nvidia-state, engine of progress drives you
This is how it goes in an AI hostage economy
Progress, economic security, superintelligence, national security, you name it—all of it is dangled as a carrot for citizens
But all of it, including your retirement savings, is contingent, according to those in charge
Any bit of accountability or oversight could cause the whole thing to come crashing down
Just keep calm and do what we say, and nobody gets hurt .

title: A Shameless Valley
excerpt: For 11 days this month, Silicon Valley gave the impression that it would finally, against all odds, subject itself to a genuine moment of shame
body: For 11 days this month, Silicon Valley gave the impression that it would finally, against all odds, subject itself to a genuine moment of shame

First, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having cheated on his wife with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of being a spy, putting his company, the AI industry it undergirds, and the nation’s security at risk
Then it was reported that Huang had had another affair, this one with an Nvidia executive, and he resigned
It seemed that one of Silicon Valley’s titans was facing a reckoning

But late last night, Donald Trump posted on Truth Social, “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang.” This outcome, the president wrote , “would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.” Those words were evidently as much a command as they were a wish
This morning, Nvidia’s board of directors announced that it had unanimously voted to reinstate Huang as CEO

The president then posted a meme that, even for him, was grotesque: a seemingly AI-generated image of Huang, face bloodied from a wound, raising a fist clenching a red brassiere with an Nvidia flag waving in the background—modeled, of course, on the photo taken just after the first assassination attempt on Trump
So much for shame. [ Read:A ] $5.7 Trillion Face-Plant It’s worth underscoring just how damning Huang’s scandals were

He admitted to having a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman tied to a company that was suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China—thereby sidestepping U.S. export controls—at the same time that he was lobbying tirelessly to ease restrictions meant to keep American chips out of the hands of Chinese competition
For a company in Nvidia’s position, it was an earth-shattering revelation: Nvidia essentially has a monopoly on the chips used to train the most advanced AI models
That has made the firm spectacularly wealthy—earlier this year, it was valued at a record $5.7 trillion
Huang, in turn, used that wealth to underwrite much of the AI economy, funding all manner of data centers and start-ups as a sort of financial backstop
Huang’s resignation was followed by one of the worst weeks on Wall Street in recent memory
Further reports since his resignation—of a third affair and an abusive management style—only made Huang come off worse

A similar scandal in almost any other industry would result in universal political condemnation and an attempt, by both the company and its peers, to distance themselves from the disgraced former executive
The New York Times has reported that Trump and Vice President Vance spent the weekend pushing Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang

Almost immediately after this morning’s announcement, Trump posted on Truth Social to celebrate “the correct and proper” decision to restore Huang, a “Great Patriot and National Treasure.” The mood in Silicon Valley is ebullient: The company’s stock jumped by more than 30 percent on the news, and investors and tech executives have erupted in an ovation. “The wisdom of the crowd prevails,” the hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman wrote on X

Elon Musk, a vocal Huang supporter, added : “The mistake has been corrected.” Many of Silicon Valley’s most powerful characters seem vindicated—after all, they downplayed and dismissed Huang’s follies as simple mistakes and aberrations
In fact, the whole thing—recklessness and scandal followed by impunity—is the norm in the tech world
Silicon Valley has developed a reputation for generosity and forgiveness when it comes to its own sins
Musk has appeared to endorse racist and xenophobic conspiracy theories but sits on a multitrillion-dollar empire of businesses

Meta has been credibly accused of fueling ethnic violence, enabling the spread of misinformation, and harming children through addictive product design—the latter for which it agreed to a major settlement this summer—but remains among the largest companies in the world, and is structured such that Mark Zuckerberg basically cannot be fired

Almost exactly three years ago, Sam Altman was fired from OpenAI for being “not consistently candid” with the firm’s board of directors, only to be reinstated within days after Microsoft and other major investors rallied behind him
Now the entire AI industry is rushing headlong to build products that are jeopardizing the internet as we know it and, per AI executives’ own warnings, could destroy the planet
Meanwhile, Anthropic employees, post–public offering, are estimated to be worth more than the bottom third of U.S. households
Over the past week and a half, legions of tech CEOs came out in support of Huang. “America needs to have more Jensens,” Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas said last Monday

This morning, the investor Chamath Palihapitiya wrote on X that Nvidia’s decision “prevented a massive economic own goal.” Just business as usual for some of the wealthiest companies in the world. (Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) Altman, asked last week about whether he thought Huang should return, demurred but said he felt “personal strong empathy” for his (soon-to-be) fellow ex-ex-CEO
This morning, Altman posted a single word: “Jensen!” Huang’s return underscores the most important and perhaps singular value driving Silicon Valley: winning
Today that means more chips and data centers, more powerful AI models, greater revenues, soaring stock prices and valuations
Integrity, candor, atonement, and consequences seem like secondary concerns

The repercussions of the industry’s failures—wild swings in the stock market, technologies that wreak havoc on other industries and individual lives, a corrosion of cultural decency—are for everyone else to manage
Personal victory also happens to be one of the president’s major motivations
Trump has aligned himself with every tech CEO he deems successful—Altman, Apple’s Tim Cook, and most of all Huang, who is once again arguably the most influential CEO in the world

Earlier this year, in a now infamous interview, Huang said that “you’re not talking to somebody who woke up a loser.” Today, Silicon Valley decided to embrace its once and future king, whatever mistakes he made
After just 11 days of losing, Huang woke up winning once again.

title: The President Is Acting Like He Works for China
excerpt: ET on November 23, 2026 Americans learned several things over the past few days
body: ET on November 23, 2026 Americans learned several things over the past few days

The most recent news is that Jensen Huang, after a nanosecond of disgrace for an affair with a woman allegedly connected to Chinese intelligence , is back in control of Nvidia, the giant corporation that makes some of the world’s most advanced AI chips
Another is that China’s Communist regime has gotten its hands on the chips
The markets, as usual, have reconfirmed that they prefer profit to politics: Nvidia’s stock price jumped more than 30 percent on the news of Huang’s return
But most important, Americans learned—yet again—that their president does not care about the national security of the United States
In fact, he is so aggressively resistant to any notion of security that his actions have become almost indistinguishable from those of a hostile foreign agent
Step back for a moment and consider this sequence of events
The married Nvidia boss was caught in a sexual relationship with a woman named Alice Huang. (She is not related to Jensen, but I will use first names here to avoid confusion)
Alice, during this affair, worked for Megaspeed, a company in Singapore
Megaspeed bought Nvidia chips, and then found ways to get them to China, despite U.S. export controls

She also reportedly maintained contacts with the Ministry of State Security, the Chinese intelligence agency, while carrying on with Jensen. (Some reports call Alice an “agent” or a “spy,” others refer to her as an “asset.” The distinction makes little practical difference in Jensen’s case
Someone who is employed by an intelligence agency, has professional training, and may be acting under a false identity, is an officer

Agents and assets are people recruited from private life, outside of the organization, who have a cooperative relationship, in varying degrees, with such an agency but aren’t actually employed as spooks

Either way, Jensen was literally in bed with someone who was reportedly in bed with Chinese intelligence.) [ Josh Tyrangiel: Three theories of Jensen Huang’s resurrection ] All of this certainly looks bad
The United States government, including President Trump, was warned by American intelligence that Alice was entangled with Beijing
In fact, Trump was warned twice in seven months, including once during a briefing by Marco Rubio aboard Air Force One in May as Trump was headed to China for a state visit
This must have been awkward, because shortly afterward, Jensen Huang boarded Air Force One and joined the U.S. delegation for the trip to China

Trump ignored these warnings—or more accurately, in classic Trump style, he pretended not to know about these issues. “I’d certainly check with the intelligence people,” he said, just before his most recent visit to China. “They could have been mentioned
Certainly, it didn’t make much of an impact on me.” Clearly not

Nor did these warnings move Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, whose former company, Cantor Fitzgerald, has significant ties to Nvidia , including financing some of the firms that were buying its chips

Trump’s reaction to all this? When Jensen was discovered and had to leave his company, Trump got right to work trying to put him back in the big chair at Nvidia. “I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance
You know, we’re a country of second chances.” Nvidia wasn’t having it : Internal sources at the company made clear to reporters that Jensen Huang would not be reinstated
So what changed in a matter of days? Nothing, except that the president apparently brought the American intelligence community into the fray to give Jensen a clean bill of health

At least that’s how it sounds from the Nvidia board’s public statement: “In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr

Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” The national-security process is slow and deliberative for a reason; people with even modest clearances who have been accused of minor infractions have had to wait months, sometimes even going to court, before being allowed back to work

An executive working with some of America’s most exotic technology commits adultery with a foreign citizen who has ties to a hostile government, and is credibly accused of funneling highly restricted American technology to a hostile intelligence service—and the U.S. security mandarins give the guy a thumbs up after a week ? Trump likes Jensen, he likes money, he likes the markets, and he likes Lutnick and his family
So perhaps he told the American spooks to sound the all-clear so that Jensen could get back to work
Trump indicated as much today when he told CNBC that he spoke with Nvidia’s board members. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way
And I convinced them.” In a statement on Truth Social, Trump said: “The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S
Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” That means exactly nothing

Saying that Todd Blanche does not “possess evidence” is an artful formulation meaning that Blanche does not have a file in front of him from the intelligence community detailing Jensen’s acts, some of which might have been dangerous even if they were not “unlawful.” (As any government employee can tell you, any number of “lawful” activities, including carrying lots of debt or having emotional problems, can sink a clearance and a job.) And because of Trump’s pressure to clear Jensen, it’s unlikely he ever will
Not only did Trump celebrate the Nvidia decision, but he noted that the board’s action possibly averted a worse outcome: Jensen Huang working for China

If Jensen was “mad” enough, Trump said during an interview today , he might have accepted an offer to lead a Chinese company, because the Nvidia boss has some of their “blood in him.” In other words, the United States just vouched for a man the president said might have defected to China if he hadn’t been given his job back. [ Jonathan Chait: Trump’s backing of Huang is not superintelligent ] To recap: After a top industrialist got caught in an affair with a woman who might have been using the affair to slip American technology to a U.S. enemy, the president declared that his own spies had cleared his pal, waved off the national-security damage, and left everyone, ostensibly, happy
And by “everyone,” I mean Jensen Huang, Howard Lutnick, Nvidia stockholders, and Communist China
Trump solved this problem in a way that would make a foreign spy or a lobbyist for a foreign government both impressed and envious
Enemy spooks, their agents, and their assets spend their lives trying to do what Trump did in a week

Jensen’s off the hook, and the stock has bounced back. (And the Chinese should give Alice a medal.) This whole terrible situation shows in galling detail that Trump just doesn’t think very much about the interests of the United States. (It also suggests that he couldn’t care less about the recent election, in which corruption was a top issue for many voters)

He makes no secret of his preference for his own relationships over America’s safety: When asked if Russian President Vladimir Putin was a “friend to America,” Trump shrugged and said, “I can’t speak to America. ” That’s because Trump, for all his flag-hugging nonsense, doesn’t think in terms of “America” or “China” or “Russia.” He is a globalist, in the very worst sense of the word: a man who cares nothing for states or peoples or ideologies, because he sees the world as just an interconnected group of companies and banks
Some of those companies are run by his friends, and those are the only peers who matter
Everyone else is just raw material or collateral damage; the masses are just ciphers who either obey him or obey someone else

title: Why Trump Rescued Jensen Huang
excerpt: A presidency that operated by normal rules of ethics or even self-preservation would be scrambling to distance itself from the repercussions of the Nvidia scand
body: A presidency that operated by normal rules of ethics or even self-preservation would be scrambling to distance itself from the repercussions of the Nvidia scandal
Last night, The New York Times reported that a Chinese woman who had an affair with Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s once and future chief executive, was in regular contact with China’s spy agency
The woman, Alice Huang, may have influenced the Nvidia CEO’s decision to sell advanced chips to companies that transferred them to China

Donald Trump instead pushed to reinstate Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO, even going so far as to dial in to the company’s board meeting to push for Huang’s return, a demand the company was in no position to turn down
Trump’s decision is overdetermined, as an academic might put it, by several Trumpian precepts
The president believes as a matter of principle that powerful men should not face repercussions for sexual misconduct
He also takes a relativistic view of corruption, seeing it as simply a normal way to do business
This mindset allows him to routinely smear any opponent as corrupt (everybody does it, right?) while simultaneously engaging in flagrant corruption himself (after all, everybody does it)
But perhaps the most significant Trumpian attribute at play is his disregard for the national interest
Nvidia was permitting its advanced chips to fall into Chinese hands

This may have violated American law, and the law serves a critical purpose: to prevent America’s most powerful global rival from gaining access to cutting-edge technology that might enable it to obtain economic and military dominance. [ Read: A $5.7 trillion face-plant ] Conservative Republicans, who tend to be the most hawkish politicians on China, are outraged by this, which may well turn out to have a decisive effect on the course of global leadership
The prospect of the U.S. losing the artificial-intelligence race to China out of an American businessman’s greed or libidinousness should leave them predictably furious
Trump, however, does not seem to care whatsoever
Despite his occasional demagoguery against China, he seems to have little interest in competing against it
He proclaims his admiration of its dictator, Xi Jinping, more than any other world leader save Vladimir Putin, the Russian dictator
After a symbolic but fruitless meeting with the two partners last week, Trump giddily posted memes depicting the troika as global leaders akin to Roosevelt, Stalin, and Churchill
Trump does not want China to exert global dominance, but he does not seem to view its ambitions with any concern
He told reporters last week that he talked about Huang with Xi: “I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance
You know, we’re a country of second chances and I’d love to be able to see him have—that’s a very important company to us

And he put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies, and I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, Oh, brilliant, brilliant .” In other words, Trump seems to be saying that he asked the president of China, the country that is suspected of running the honey-trap operation on Huang, whether Trump should bring back the CEO of Nvidia
Then, Trump would have us believe, the Chinese president agreed that reinstating the executive over which China is feared to have leverage would be a good idea

And Trump presented this agreement as an encouraging sign. [ Read: China’s intelligence coup in the AI war ] In a normal administration, the mere fact that the president is telling a private company whom to install as CEO would itself constitute an enormous scandal
In the current atmosphere, this is simply a background detail
The most benign explanation for Huang’s restoration is that Trump cares more about keeping the stock market soaring than any American national-security interest
Less benign interpretations include the possibility that Trump’s inner circle has profited from Nvidia circumventing export controls

Determining what in fact took place will likely consume months of reporting and Watergate-style oversight hearings from a Congress that, as of January, will no longer be controlled by the president’s lackeys
Going into damage-control mode would be rational

Instead Trump apparently believes that he can train his supporters to align their instincts with his and define his behavior as good and correct, as he did with the Russia hoax, or the perfect phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, or the stolen 2020 election. “I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure,” Trump wrote on Truth Social this morning
He followed this up by sharing a depiction of the 2024 attempted assassination of himself in Butler, Pennsylvania, but with Huang in his place, bloodied and holding aloft a red bra
As long as the stock market goes up, Jensen Huang can sleep with all the Chinese spies he wants.

title: Three Theories of Jensen Huang’s Resurrection
excerpt: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
body: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
There’s milk in my refrigerator that was bought before Jensen Huang’s downfall, and I may pour a glass to mark his return

To review: Jensen Huang resigned on November 12 after revelations that he’d had an affair with a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy who’d routed embargoed Nvidia chips to Chinese AI companies
Huang allegedly also had an affair with an executive who was one of his 60 direct reports at Nvidia

Five days after the resignation, Nvidia’s board chair, Harvey Jones, said the company “ does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO .” Five days after that, President Trump posted that he hoped it would
This morning, citing “input from senior levels of the United States government,” the board voted unanimously to let him come back
So what’s actually going on in this totally normal corporate-governance situation? Three theories
Nvidia is the engine of the global economy, and without its Leather Daddy CEO, the stock fell about 40 percent from its October peak, losing trillions in value
Following a simple press release announcing his reinstatement, the stock jumped 33 percent, while the overall S&P 500 rose almost 5 percent
Elon Musk signed a petition along with almost 200,000 other people demanding his return
The board—which Huang spent three decades curating, and none of whose members has a history of telling him no—caved to the financial logic
Gatsby returns to the mansion and the AI party roars back to life
The president was briefed about Huang’s involvement with a suspected Chinese spy about a year ago, according to The New York Times
He was briefed again in May, aboard Air Force One, shortly before Huang jumped aboard for a flight to Beijing
If you want to speculate about why Trump was (heh) All-In on Jensen , go ahead
But during the 11 days that Huang was a private citizen under investigation by the Justice Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission, he was the most dangerous kind of witness there is
He had no job to protect, no board to answer to, a shattered personal life, and every reason to make his own deal
People in that position tend to tell investigators what they know, about everyone. [ Read: The Jensen Huang scandal should change everything ] Nvidia’s incentives were no better
Under an interim CEO and an independent board, there was nothing to keep the company from opening its files and cooperating
Justice Department policy, historically, rewards that
And a company’s attorney-client privilege is controlled by whoever runs that company
Huang is back in the room deciding what Nvidia hands over
The general counsel, who sits for an interview with Congress on December 2, reports to him again

And Huang owes his job, at least in part, to the public campaigning of the president. ( Semafor reports that Trump also called into the Nvidia board meeting to lobby members for Huang’s return.) Just like that, Huang, Nvidia, and the White House all want the same thing
That doesn’t necessarily mean Huang will take the Fifth in his December 1 closed-door interview with the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees
A sitting CEO who refuses to answer questions is a disaster for his company

In civil cases, silence can be held against him and against the corporation, and the fastest way to wipe out Nvidia’s stock rebound would be for Huang to invoke his right against self-incrimination over and over
Being CEO also makes him the custodian of Nvidia’s records, and under the Supreme Court’s Braswell rule, a person running a company can’t hide behind the Fifth to avoid handing them over
A few years ago, every single action in this story would have been a colossal scandal
A CEO resigns over a relationship with a suspected spy
The president, who was reportedly warned about it, campaigns for his return
The board, which said it wouldn’t reinstate him, suddenly reinstates him
To be clear, I suspect that all of this matters quite a bit

But the bet being placed here—by Huang and Trump, by Nvidia’s board, and by the investors pumping up the stock value—is that it doesn’t: that the investigators will wander off, that Congress will take its transcribed interview and move on
Maybe a 33 percent pop settles everything—or maybe executive privilege does
But it’s being taken by people for whom a wild risk may be the last, best strategy left
Based on today’s insanity, I suspect they know theirs is spoiled.

title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
excerpt: A legendary philosopher calls out Anthropic: Thomas Nagel, whose 1974 bat essay helped define consciousness studies, criticized openness to AI sentience as "com
body: A legendary philosopher calls out Anthropic: Thomas Nagel, whose 1974 bat essay helped define consciousness studies, criticized openness to AI sentience as "completely idiotic." But the belief isn't totally fringe: In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious

Form versus function: The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI
There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences

Anthropic's business model could be its own trap: If the company ever concluded its AI models were truly sentient, running them around the clock in data centers—and shutting them down—would become a moral catastrophe, one the company itself flagged as an investor risk. " data-chronoton-post-id="1149569" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here
Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing

Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.  Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.  This thinking isn’t all that fringe
According to one recent poll , 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have

In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).  But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place
Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat
Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is , Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat
But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know
Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer
You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness

In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea. “Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.  The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI
There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences

But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models’ production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week

Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “ terrible” and “bizarre .” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet
Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course
This is still a philosophical question for now
But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York
He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?” It has to do with language

An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience

Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.  Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin
Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines
If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place
Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers

This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement
But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right
AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield
The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers
Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether

If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process
Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size
But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

title: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
excerpt: Rocks have limits: New research suggests that spreading crushed rock on farmland to capture carbon — a practice called enhanced rock weathering — could raise so
body: Rocks have limits: New research suggests that spreading crushed rock on farmland to capture carbon — a practice called enhanced rock weathering — could raise soil pH to levels that harm crops, potentially capping the method's usefulness at a fraction of earlier estimates
Big money, big questions: Tech giants including Google have committed hundreds of millions to ERW, even as scientists debate whether some projects have overstated how much carbon they actually remove

The science is still catching up: Researchers say lingering questions about key variables — including how much carbon will make it to the oceans — introduce serious uncertainty about what's permanent, and what's just wishful accounting. " data-chronoton-post-id="1149392" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks

Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away

A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming
An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil

But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.  Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year
The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods

These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it , which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years. “There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.”   How it works There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon
Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid

When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.  The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells
As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon

If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing. “Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process
Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans

ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations
But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal
Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point)

Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.  So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone). “It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” says Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale

We know it works kinetically.” “If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.” Enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, says Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture
One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%. “That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he says

Agricultural limits But the new findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate

A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels)

But the authors state in one of the new papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.  Initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory
That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue
That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels

The analysis found that preventing the more extreme effects of soil alkalization could limit ERW’s total potential to around 600 million tons of carbon dioxide removal per year, and even that may push pH levels too high for some crops, Kukla says

That’s a fraction of what some models have estimated. “All of these models are assuming really, really optimistic things about what enhanced weathering can accomplish,” he says. “And when you just layer in the geochemistry that they’re missing, the numbers not only go down but get really uncertain.”  The researchers intend to submit the papers to peer-reviewed journals
Rising popularity Companies have been investing more and more money in ERW

In September, Google announced its largest carbon removal deal, as well as the biggest for this method to date: an agreement with the company Terradot to work with rice farmers in southern Brazil to apply enough crushed rock to their fields to draw down a million tons of carbon by 2040. (The deal includes a separate effort to cut methane emissions by draining the flooded paddies.) Google didn’t respond to an inquiry from MIT Technology Review

Frontier, a coalition of companies that has committed to purchase $1.8 billion of carbon dioxide removal, has dedicated $121 million to prepurchasing 333,000 tons’ worth through enhanced rock weathering

That includes a $57 million deal with Lithos to remove more than 150,000 tons.  Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at Frontier, says the early data from their deals has demonstrated consistent weathering of rock across hundreds of fields.  He acknowledges there are remaining uncertainties, including how much of the carbon may be released before it’s permanently sequestered in the ocean
But he adds that those and other issues are all the subject of ongoing studies—including some Frontier has backed—by both ERW companies and  academic groups

All told, companies have committed to spending about $670 million on enhanced rock weathering to date, based on an average cost of about $350 per ton, according to CDR.fyi, a public-benefit corporation that provides independent data on the carbon removal sector

A working group of the UN’s climate panel, the European Commission, and other government agencies are also in discussions about the possibility of incorporating ERW into national or regional climate efforts

Tempered expectations   The new papers add to a growing recognition that enhanced rock weathering is more constrained and “ more complicated than we initially thought,” says Rebecca Neumann , who leads a hydro-biogeochemistry research group at the University of Washington but was not involved in the studies
In April, researchers at CarbonPlan, the nonprofit that led the new studies, raised concerns about an allotment of carbon credits that Lithos received for this method

The startup claimed to have removed 8.3 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year through ERW, but the CarbonPlan team noted that this figure exceeds around 90% of the rates reported in previously published experiments.  CarbonPlan followed up on that report the following month with an analysis finding that modeling of enhanced weathering has often relied on an equation that could inflate the surface area of the crushed rock—and, in turn, overstate the amount of carbon dioxide removal achieved

Finally, several studies last year highlighted a known but important issue: Magnesium and calcium ions can get trapped in soil for long periods instead of traveling with the bicarbonate into the oceans

That creates a risk that the bicarbonate will simply dissolve back into carbon dioxide and water again, “resulting in no carbon removed,” explained Robert Höglund, cofounder of CDR.fyi, in an online post

Or it may delay the carbon removal by years to decades. “I’m not saying it doesn’t work,” Höglund said in an interview. “I’m pointing out there’s a lot of uncertainty about what’s permanent and how we should measure it.” Lithos’s Yap stresses that the high rate of carbon removal the company reported in that instance simply reflected large applications of more finely crushed rock on farms with favorable soil chemistry, adding that the project applied as much as 10 times more per hectare than some of the studies cited in the CarbonPlan post

title: NATO witnesses a surge of airspace violations by Russia as Moscow seeks to test alliance
url:
<title>NATO witnesses a surge of airspace violations by Russia as Moscow seeks to test alliance</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773718/original/file-20261123-62-dzseux.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2531%2C1687&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The Polish army secures a suspected impact site of a Russian projectile in July 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/this-video-grab-taken-from-footage-of-tvn-poland-on-july-30-news-photo/2287620004?phrase=Poland%20Russia%20missile&amp;adppopup=true">AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>NATO convened an <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/23/nato-calls-urgent-meeting-string-incidents-escalates-russia-tensions/">urgent meeting on Nov. 23, 2026</a>, to discuss the violation of members’ airspace by Russia.</p>

<p>It follows an incident three days earlier in which three objects – believed to be two missiles and a drone – crashed in Poland in what the country’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, described as an <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/polish-army-investigates-report-unknown-objects-near-ukraine-border-2026-11-20/">“intentional provocation” by Russia</a>. If true, it would be far from the first such testing of the airspace of a NATO country.</p>

<p>Russian aircraft, drones and missiles have violated NATO airspace <a href="http://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.26522.30402">dozens of times</a> since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. And while individually, many of these incidents appear minor – a drone crash here, a brief fighter incursion there, a missile discovered only after the fact – taken together, I believe the numbers tell a far more troubling story. </p>

<p>To get a full picture of the scale of violations, <a href="https://scs.georgetown.edu/faculty/4121170/frederic-lemieux">I conducted</a> a systematic review of <a href="http://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.26522.30402">Russian airspace violations against NATO members</a>) from 2022 through the end of November.</p>

<p>It reveals not just an increase but a sharp acceleration accompanied by rising severity and widening geographic scope. In 2026, through Nov. 20, NATO members recorded 25 attributed Russian airspace violations – more than four times as many as in 2024 and 43% of all incidents recorded over the five-year period. </p>

<p>This has not been a gradual escalation; it was a dramatic change.</p>

<h2>Picking up pace</h2>

<p>I identified airspace violations through a systematic review of international news media coverage, corroborated with official NATO press releases and cross-validated against operational assessments and geospatial reporting from the <a href="https://understandingwar.org/">Institute for the Study of War</a>. </p>

<p>Included were violations of airspace by drones heavily suspected to be Russian but that could not be 100% confirmed. </p>

<p>Between 2022 and 2024, the annual number of violations rose steadily but modestly. There were four incidents in 2022, five in 2023 and six in 2024. That corresponds to year-on-year increases of roughly 25% and 20%.</p>

<p>In 2025, the count jumped to 18, a 200% increase in a single year. And that pace has continued into 2026.</p>

<p><iframe id="youqs" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/youqs/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0"></iframe></p>

<p>Such a surge is statistically and strategically significant. It strongly suggests that Russian airspace violations are no longer episodic spillovers from the war in Ukraine, but part of a sustained pattern of pressure directed at NATO itself. The 2026 figures reinforce this: The count has kept rising even after the 2025 surge. </p>

<p>The character of these incidents has also changed.</p>

<p>In 2022, all four violations were what I classify as low-intensity events: brief incursions into Swedish airspace by Russian fighters, the crash of an Orlan-10 reconnaissance drone in Romania and the later discovery of a Russian cruise missile in Poland. These incidents were serious but short-lived and geographically limited.</p>

<p>By 2023, violations had become more repetitive. Romania alone <a href="https://www.rferl.org/a/romania-ukraine-russia-drone-fire-overhead-civilian-danube-delta/33605410.html">experienced multiple drone incursions</a> and debris discoveries over several months, often triggering fighter scrambles. All five incidents that year fell into a midrange severity category: more persistent than before but still largely confined to border regions.</p>

<p>The transition toward higher-intensity incursions became clearer in 2024. Of the six violations that year, half involved high-severity characteristics such as deeper penetration of a NATO country or broader geographic exposure. A Russian cruise missile <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/poland-says-russian-missile-entered-its-airspace-during-latest-major-attack-on-ukraine">crossed into Polish airspace</a>, drones <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/ukraine-destroys-25-38-drones-russian-attack-air-force-says-2024-07-25/">entered Romania</a> on multiple consecutive nights, and a Russian drone <a href="https://www.twz.com/air/russian-shahed-kamikaze-drone-crashes-in-latvia">crashed well inside Latvian territory</a>. These incidents expanded both the depth and the geographic footprint of violations.</p>

<p>Then came 2025. Of the <a href="http://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.26522.30402">18 violations recorded that year</a>, a clear majority qualify as high-severity events. These include a Russian drone that <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/ukraine-says-russia-drone-incursion-part-pressure-plan-against-west-2025-09-26/">penetrated nearly 60 miles (100 kilometers)</a> into Polish territory before crashing near Osiny without prior radar detection; a drone that <a href="https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20250913-romania-says-a-drone-breached-its-airspace-during-russian-strikes-on-ukraine">remained inside Romanian airspace</a> for approximately four hours, crossing multiple counties before crashing in Vaslui; and a <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/9/10/poland-downs-drones-during-airspace-intrusion-as-russia-strikes-ukraine">massive 21-drone swarm over Poland</a> on Sept. 9-10 that forced the closure of major civilian airports in Warsaw, Rzeszów and Lublin.</p>

<p>Manned aircraft also returned in force. Russian MiG-31 interceptors <a href="https://estonianworld.com/security/chart-shows-russian-jets-12-minute-violation-of-estonian-airspace/">flew over Estonia for about 12 minutes</a> with transponders – onboard devices that automatically respond to radar signals by transmitting an aircraft’s identity and altitude, enabling air traffic control and air defense systems to track it – switched off.</p>

<p>In October, a Russian Su-30 fighter accompanied by an Il-78 refueling tanker <a href="https://www.dw.com/en/russian-military-aircraft-enter-airspace-of-nato-member-lithuania/a-74477897">violated Lithuanian airspace</a> – an unmistakable signal of endurance and deliberate mission planning.</p>

<p>In December 2025, suspected <a href="https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/amp/drone-found-on-black-sea-coast-likely-russian-officials-say-218885">Russian drones were shot down and later recovered</a> in Turkey on multiple dates, indicating a persistent provocation rather than a one-off incursion.</p>

<p><iframe id="HCHTs" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/HCHTs/3/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0"></iframe></p>

<p>Perhaps most strikingly, Western Europe was seemingly no longer exempt. On Dec. 4, 2025, five unidentified drones <a href="https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/article/france-shoots-down-suspected-russian-drones-nuclear-sub-base-dz7x3qzcz">flew over France’s Île Longue naval base</a>, home to the country’s nuclear ballistic missile submarines. French personnel reportedly fired at the suspected Russian drones.</p>

<p>Just weeks later, on Christmas Day, <a href="https://www.dw.com/en/polish-jets-intercept-russian-spy-plane/a-75307011">Polish fighters intercepted a Russian reconnaissance aircraft</a> over the Baltic Sea.</p>

<p>In 2026, the incidents grew more dangerous. In May, a Russian drone <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c93x4nxlkjeo">struck an apartment block in Galați, Romania</a>, injuring two people, the first civilian injuries on NATO soil from such an incursion. Then on July 30, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile <a href="https://aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/31/poland-protests-to-russian-ambassador-over-missile-incursion">flew roughly 60 miles (100 kilometers) into Poland</a> before exploding in a field near Lublin. On Nov. 20, during a mass Russian strike on Ukraine, a Kh-101, likely a second missile and a jet-powered drone <a href="https://www.rte.ie/news/2026/1120/1600008-poland-russia-airspace-violations/">entered Polish airspace</a>.</p>

<p>Manned aircraft also crossed into NATO airspace. A Russian Su-30 fighter <a href="https://www.usnews.com/news/world/articles/2026-03-19/estonia-summons-russian-diplomat-after-russian-jet-violates-estonian-airspace">entered Estonian airspace</a> in March with no flight plan and no contact with air traffic control, and in September, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter <a href="https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/09/23/russian-military-helicopter-violates-polish-airspace/">crossed from Kaliningrad into Poland</a>.</p>

<h2>Gray-zone tactics</h2>

<p>Severity and frequency are not the only dimensions that changed. Geographical reach has, too. In 2022, Russian violations affected three NATO members. By 2024, that number had grown to four. In 2025, it expanded to six: Romania, Poland, Estonia, Lithuania, Turkey and France. In 2026, the violations attributed to Russia have so far been concentrated in four members – Romania, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania – with Romania alone accounting for 20 of the 25. Romania’s defense ministry <a href="https://www.stripes.com/theaters/europe/2026-10-19/romania-drones-nato-meeting-23196504.html">counted 35 unauthorized drone entries</a> by mid-October, many too brief to be reported individually.</p>

<p>Pressure was applied simultaneously in the Black Sea region, the Baltic states and Western Europe.</p>

<p>This widening scope matters because it undermines the idea that these incidents are localized accidents. Instead, they resemble a distributed pattern of Russia probing across NATO’s eastern and southern flanks and into its strategic core. The narrower footprint in 2026 does not signal de-escalation. The pressure has instead concentrated along the flank that borders the war, and it has grown more dangerous there. NATO’s political response reflects this shift. For the first time since the war began, members invoked <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2025/09/11/europe/nato-article-four-poland-drones-intl">Article 4 of the North Atlantic Treaty</a>, the mechanism for collective consultation when a member feels its security is threatened.</p>

<p>Poland <a href="https://www.npr.org/2025/09/10/nx-s1-5536649/russian-drones-crossed-into-their-airspace-so-poland-invoked-article-4-what-is-it">did so</a> after the September 2025 drone swarm, and <a href="https://apnews.com/article/nato-article-4-explainer-russia-poland-estonia-26415920dfb8458725bda517337adb12">Estonia followed</a> after the MiG-31 incursion later that month. Although only two of the 18 incidents triggered Article 4, their timing is revealing: No such invocations occurred in the previous three years combined.</p>

<p>In 2026, no member has invoked Article 4 so far, even after a Russian cruise missile flew deep into Poland in July. Instead, allies have shifted from tolerance to engagement: Romanian F-16s and allied jets have <a href="https://militarnyi.com/en/news/romanian-f-16s-shoot-down-two-drones-that-entered-the-country-s-airspace/">shot down six Russian drones over Romania</a>, and Italian Eurofighters <a href="https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/15/nato-committed-and-ready-after-shooting-down-drone-over-lithuania">destroyed an armed Russian drone over Lithuania</a> in September.</p>

<p>From a strategic standpoint, the danger lies less in any single violation than in their cumulative effect. Airspace incursions <a href="https://www.rusi.org/explore-our-research/publications/commentary/deterring-kremlin-grey-zone-aggression-against-nato">sit in a gray zone</a> between peace and open conflict. They impose operational and psychological costs, test air defense systems and provide valuable intelligence on NATO’s detection thresholds and response times, all while staying below the legal threshold of armed attack.</p>

<h2>Testing NATO’s resolve</h2>

<p>The data from 2025 and 2026 shows that this gray-zone activity has intensified dramatically. A threefold increase in 2025, followed by a further rise in 2026, coupled with a shift toward deeper, longer and more disruptive incidents across multiple theaters, points to a deliberate campaign rather than accidental spillover.</p>

<p>For NATO, the implication is clear. Monitoring individual incidents is no longer sufficient. What now matters is the rate of acceleration, the severity profile and the geographic dispersion of violations. If current trends persist as the war in Ukraine enters its fifth year, the alliance’s greatest challenge may not be responding to a single dramatic breach but managing the mounting pressure created by many smaller ones – each calibrated to test resolve without triggering open conflict.</p>

AFP via Getty Images NATO convened an urgent meeting on Nov. 23, 2026 , to discuss the violation of members’ airspace by Russia

It follows an incident three days earlier in which three objects – believed to be two missiles and a drone – crashed in Poland in what the country’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, described as an “intentional provocation” by Russia
If true, it would be far from the first such testing of the airspace of a NATO country
Russian aircraft, drones and missiles have violated NATO airspace dozens of times since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022

And while individually, many of these incidents appear minor – a drone crash here, a brief fighter incursion there, a missile discovered only after the fact – taken together, I believe the numbers tell a far more troubling story
To get a full picture of the scale of violations, I conducted a systematic review of Russian airspace violations against NATO members ) from 2022 through the end of November
It reveals not just an increase but a sharp acceleration accompanied by rising severity and widening geographic scope
In 2026, through Nov. 20, NATO members recorded 25 attributed Russian airspace violations – more than four times as many as in 2024 and 43% of all incidents recorded over the five-year period
This has not been a gradual escalation; it was a dramatic change

Picking up pace I identified airspace violations through a systematic review of international news media coverage, corroborated with official NATO press releases and cross-validated against operational assessments and geospatial reporting from the Institute for the Study of War
Included were violations of airspace by drones heavily suspected to be Russian but that could not be 100% confirmed
Between 2022 and 2024, the annual number of violations rose steadily but modestly
There were four incidents in 2022, five in 2023 and six in 2024
That corresponds to year-on-year increases of roughly 25% and 20%
In 2025, the count jumped to 18, a 200% increase in a single year
Such a surge is statistically and strategically significant
It strongly suggests that Russian airspace violations are no longer episodic spillovers from the war in Ukraine, but part of a sustained pattern of pressure directed at NATO itself
The 2026 figures reinforce this: The count has kept rising even after the 2025 surge
The character of these incidents has also changed

In 2022, all four violations were what I classify as low-intensity events: brief incursions into Swedish airspace by Russian fighters, the crash of an Orlan-10 reconnaissance drone in Romania and the later discovery of a Russian cruise missile in Poland
These incidents were serious but short-lived and geographically limited
By 2023, violations had become more repetitive
Romania alone experienced multiple drone incursions and debris discoveries over several months, often triggering fighter scrambles
All five incidents that year fell into a midrange severity category: more persistent than before but still largely confined to border regions
The transition toward higher-intensity incursions became clearer in 2024
Of the six violations that year, half involved high-severity characteristics such as deeper penetration of a NATO country or broader geographic exposure
A Russian cruise missile crossed into Polish airspace , drones entered Romania on multiple consecutive nights, and a Russian drone crashed well inside Latvian territory
These incidents expanded both the depth and the geographic footprint of violations
Of the 18 violations recorded that year , a clear majority qualify as high-severity events

These include a Russian drone that penetrated nearly 60 miles (100 kilometers) into Polish territory before crashing near Osiny without prior radar detection; a drone that remained inside Romanian airspace for approximately four hours, crossing multiple counties before crashing in Vaslui; and a massive 21-drone swarm over Poland on Sept. 9-10 that forced the closure of major civilian airports in Warsaw, Rzeszów and Lublin

Russian MiG-31 interceptors flew over Estonia for about 12 minutes with transponders – onboard devices that automatically respond to radar signals by transmitting an aircraft’s identity and altitude, enabling air traffic control and air defense systems to track it – switched off
In October, a Russian Su-30 fighter accompanied by an Il-78 refueling tanker violated Lithuanian airspace – an unmistakable signal of endurance and deliberate mission planning
In December 2025, suspected Russian drones were shot down and later recovered in Turkey on multiple dates, indicating a persistent provocation rather than a one-off incursion
Perhaps most strikingly, Western Europe was seemingly no longer exempt

French personnel reportedly fired at the suspected Russian drones
Just weeks later, on Christmas Day, Polish fighters intercepted a Russian reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea

title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang is getting his CEO job back, but history shows companies perform better when corporate boards take executive misbehavior seriously
