<title>Nvidia’s Jensen Huang is getting his CEO job back, but history shows companies perform better when corporate boards take executive misbehavior seriously</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773685/original/file-20261123-62-2aaryt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3799%2C2532&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">President Donald Trump is among those who pushed to have Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/president-donald-trump-greets-nvidia-ceo-jensen-huang-as-news-photo/2297774940?phrase=huang%20trump">Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis.</p>

<p>This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the <a href="https://www.wsj.com/business/nvidia-is-preparing-to-oust-nvidia-ceo-jensen-huang-30f421ad">Nov. 12, 2026, ouster of its CEO</a>, Jensen Huang, who remarkably <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/23/technology/nvidia-jensen-huang-reinstated">returned to his job</a> just 11 days later. But it <a href="https://knowledge.insead.edu/leadership-organisations/mark-hurd-affair">actually transpired over 15 years ago</a> at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd.</p>

<p>Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs – albeit in his case temporarily – over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/17/nvidia-jensen-huang-succession-board-lessons.html">shifting from his behavior to his board</a> – and the decisions that led to his exit. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.wsj.com/tech/the-campaign-to-bring-back-jensen-huang-as-nvidia-ceo-e91b0b2c">Prominent industry leaders</a> <a href="https://www.wsj.com/business/nvidias-board-not-considering-reinstating-jensen-huang-as-ceo-a2b913b1">are questioning</a> the board’s original decision to oust him. <a href="https://www.cbc.ca/news/business/nvidia-ceo-huang-calls-reinstatements-9.7423555">They include</a> Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan – <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/23/trump-nvidia-jensen-huang.html">not to mention President Donald Trump</a>, who reportedly <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/us/politics/trump-nvidia-huang.html">directed the effort</a> to get Huang reinstated. </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Ba6zwJQAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">scholar of management</a> who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board had made the right call to force him out. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, <a href="https://doi.org/10.5465/AMBPP.2017.16401abstract">I have repeatedly found</a> that doing nothing, as a board, <a href="https://oaktrust.library.tamu.edu/items/18703a1c-50be-4f9b-aa94-016212e01ddf">is worse</a> than doing something.</p>

<p>CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization. </p>

<p>But <a href="https://hbr.org/2026/11/how-boards-detect-and-prevent-internal-misconduct">it’s still hard</a> for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. This is likely why the board chose to reinstate Jensen Huang. And why his return sets a terrible precedent.</p>

<h2>The costs of misconduct</h2>

<p>One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct <a href="https://oaktrust.library.tamu.edu/items/18703a1c-50be-4f9b-aa94-016212e01ddf">exit at a significantly higher rate</a> than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because <a href="https://oaktrust.library.tamu.edu/items/18703a1c-50be-4f9b-aa94-016212e01ddf">they’re forced out</a> due to poor performance, my research shows. </p>

<p>One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/best-buy-founder-resigns-as-chairman-after-ceo-probe/">stepped down as chairman</a> of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Then-American Airlines CEO Doug Parker speaks behind a microphone as he testifies before senators on December 15, 2021, in Washington, DC" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772860/original/file-20261118-64-8g54ty.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772860/original/file-20261118-64-8g54ty.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772860/original/file-20261118-64-8g54ty.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772860/original/file-20261118-64-8g54ty.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772860/original/file-20261118-64-8g54ty.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772860/original/file-20261118-64-8g54ty.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772860/original/file-20261118-64-8g54ty.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker attracted much more negative attention after his second DUI arrest compared to his first.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/american-airlines-ceo-doug-parker-testifies-before-the-news-photo/1237251103?phrase=American%20Airlines%20CEO%20Doug%20Parker&amp;adppopup=true">Chip Somodevilla/POOL/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Directors are also <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/01492063231225420">personally penalized</a> for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may <a href="https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2006.23478165">lose their board seats</a> or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct <a href="https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2008.32626007">may spill over</a> to damage the reputations of those companies as well. </p>

<p>In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it. </p>

<p>In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/17/nvidia-creates-board-committee-to-oversee-export-controls">potential national security risks</a>.</p>

<p>Another issue is <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/moral-hazard">moral hazard</a>: when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation.</p>

<p>My research has found that risk to be high. </p>

<p>When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance <a href="https://hdl.handle.net/1969.1/156941">is often even worse</a> than the first.  </p>

<p>Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2007/02/11/us-airways-ceo-had-previous-drunk-driving-incidents-report.html">prompting criticism of the board</a> for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991.</p>

<p>Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was <a href="https://www.wsj.com/business/why-do-boards-keep-giving-misbehaving-ceos-second-chances-228db0b7">recently ousted</a> as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship.</p>

<p>In the case of Nvidia, Jensen <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/technology/jensen-huang-nvidia-board.html">reportedly lied</a> to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future?  </p>

<p>In reinstating him, the <a href="https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-board-reinstates-jensen-huang-as-president-ceo-and-board-director">board said</a> it “was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.”</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A black-and-white photo shows Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang looking on during a press briefing in Paris on October 13, 2026." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773662/original/file-20261123-76-ejed8y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C57%2C1920%2C1080&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773662/original/file-20261123-76-ejed8y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773662/original/file-20261123-76-ejed8y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773662/original/file-20261123-76-ejed8y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773662/original/file-20261123-76-ejed8y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773662/original/file-20261123-76-ejed8y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773662/original/file-20261123-76-ejed8y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Nvidia’s board has come under more scrutiny for its own oversight after it ousted, then reinstated, its CEO, Jensen Huang.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/co-founder-president-and-ceo-of-us-technology-company-news-photo/2299493247?phrase=nvidia%20board%20directors&amp;adppopup=true">Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>A question of culture</h2>

<p>Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake. </p>

<p>CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s <a href="https://hdl.handle.net/1969.1/156941">often associated</a> with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive.</p>

<p>Take <a href="https://www.wsj.com/articles/american-apparel-gets-restraining-order-against-ex-ceo-charney-1433246872">Dov Charney’s tenure</a> as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees.</p>

<p>It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U.S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. The board is likely looking at the totality of the issues and not just the personal misconduct.</p>

<p>In the runup to Huang’s return to Nvidia, the public debate had largely been centered on what the company might lose without Jensen Huang at the helm. An equally important question, though, is what the company and its board might risk by retaining a CEO whose conduct has raised serious questions about judgment, trust and organizational oversight.</p>

<p>The decision to reinstate him suggests that political pressure can interfere with companies’ hiring and firing for misconduct, and that powerful CEOs are above the normal corporate considerations that would lead to dismissal. The Nvidia case might set a precedent, as other CEOs and boards now know the playbook for getting away with misconduct.</p>

<p>It’s a board’s duty to protect its organization from managers who go astray, as legendary investor <a href="https://hbr.org/2026/11/how-boards-detect-and-prevent-internal-misconduct">Warren Buffett noted</a>: “It isn’t fundamental dishonesty that causes people to go in a different direction. It’s human nature. There are plenty of people who are really decent people, intelligent people. … But they just don’t come to grips with reality. And boards usually don’t push them to.”</p>

    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770149/original/file-20261104-64-2lkaub.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=143%2C455%2C2647%2C1764&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Nobody knows for sure what the first animal was, but likely it was small, soft and ocean-dwelling – like this comb jelly, but simpler.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/blackwater-shot-of-a-bioluminescent-comb-jelly-royalty-free-image/2286500715">Rob Atherton/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure>

<p><em><a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/curious-kids-us-74795">Curious Kids</a> is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to <a href="mailto:curiouskidsus@theconversation.com">CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com</a>.</em></p>

<hr>

<blockquote>
<p><strong>What was the first animal on Earth? – Keira, age 10, Eugene, Oregon, and Julian, age 7, South Bend, Indiana</strong></p>
</blockquote>

<hr>

<p>Imagine climbing into a time machine and setting the dial for when the very first animal was alive. You would need to travel really, really far back in time.</p>

<p>You would blow past the dinosaurs, which <a href="https://www.amnh.org/dinosaurs/dinosaur-facts">showed up about 230 million years ago</a>. Keep going and you’d pass coil-shelled <a href="https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/what-is-an-ammonite.html">ammonites</a> that swam in the oceans starting 450 million years ago, and then <a href="https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/how-trilobites-conquered-prehistoric-oceans.html">trilobites</a>, armored animals that scuttled across the seafloor more than 520 million years ago. Further still, around 558 million years ago, you would meet <em><a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aat7228">Dickinsonia</a></em>, a tiny, flat, ribbed oval only a few millimeters thick that looks more like a squashed pancake than any animal you know.</p>

<p>And even <em>Dickinsonia</em> was almost certainly not the first animal.</p>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=UvN4AQsdfygC&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=sra">We are biologists</a> <a href="http://scholar.google.com/citations?user=rBfI91QAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">who study</a> single-celled life called <a href="https://www.britannica.com/science/protist">protists</a>. How complex life such as human beings showed up in the first place is one of the major questions in our field.</p>

<p>Honestly, nobody can name the first animal, but there are many clues about what it was probably like.</p>

<h2>What makes an animal an animal?</h2>

<p>If we asked you what an animal is, you might say something that moves, eats and reproduces. The trouble is that plenty of nonanimals do all three.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/TRfPo53EuZc?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Amoebae aren’t animals.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>For instance, single-celled <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amoeba">amoebae</a> crawl, hunt and swallow their prey whole – and they are not animals at all!</p>

<p>Biologists <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal">define an animal</a> as an organism made of many cells that stick together, communicate and divide up the work of growing, eating and moving. Different types of cells specialize to do different jobs, and they all work together as one organism. And when animals eat, they take in outside material instead of making their own food from sunlight the way plants do.</p>

<p>Notice what is not on that list: Legs. Eyes. A brain. A mouth. That matters for what comes next.</p>

<h2>Consider the sea sponge</h2>

<p>SpongeBob SquarePants is a cartoon version of a real animal, the <a href="https://www.britannica.com/animal/sponge-animal">sea sponge</a>. Real sponges do not wear square pants; they don’t even move around. They sit anchored to the seafloor, pumping seawater through thousands of tiny holes and straining out bacteria to eat. They have <a href="https://www.youtube.com/shorts/wZ-aISM9pIA">no brain, no heart and no muscles</a>. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/pdpKmDZx35I?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Sponges are one super-simple animal.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>But sponges are still animals, and scientists often think of them as the simplest ones. Part of what makes them so interesting is a type of cell they have <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choanocyte">called choanocytes</a>. Each choanocyte has a whiplike tail ringed by tiny fingerlike projections that trap food.</p>

<p>Choanocytes look almost exactly like <a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3000226">choanoflagellates</a>, free-living, single-celled organisms that are the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/s0960-9822(02)01187-9">closest living relatives of animals</a>. Watching a colony of choanoflagellates feed together is about as close as you can get to seeing the doorway between single-celled life and animal life.</p>

<h2>Or were comb jellies first?</h2>

<p>Imagine climbing down the animal tree of life going backward in time. You can start with animals alive today, which would be the leaves of the tree. Branches join where you encounter ancestors shared by different groups. Follow them far enough, and they all meet at a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1098/rsob.200359">common ancestor of living animals</a>. Scientists disagree about which groups belong on each side of that deepest branching point.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770145/original/file-20261104-64-mfemsp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="two simple family trees, one showing sponges branching off first, the other showing comb jellies first" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770145/original/file-20261104-64-mfemsp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770145/original/file-20261104-64-mfemsp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770145/original/file-20261104-64-mfemsp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770145/original/file-20261104-64-mfemsp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770145/original/file-20261104-64-mfemsp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770145/original/file-20261104-64-mfemsp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770145/original/file-20261104-64-mfemsp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Two alternative family trees illustrate the evolutionary scenarios of sponges or comb jellies being the first animal on Earth.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Matthew W. Brown</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Some studies put <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2017.02.031">sponges alone on one side of that fork</a>, with every other living animal group, including us, on the other. Other studies put <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-05936-6">comb jellies in that position</a>. In that case, these shimmering, jellylike ocean swimmers would occupy one side, while sponges and all other animals would occupy the other. This is what scientists mean when they describe either group as having “branched off first.”</p>

<p>It is important to remember that “branched off first” does not mean “unchanged.” Sponges, comb jellies and humans have <a href="https://theconversation.com/no-animal-alive-today-is-primitive-why-are-so-many-still-labeled-that-way-266208">all been evolving for the same amount of time</a>, since our shared ancestor lived. Each lineage has followed its own evolutionary path, which over time has led to the great diversity of animals we see today, such as worms, insects, crabs and primates. Today’s sponges and comb jellies may therefore look very different from that common ancestor, making it difficult to picture what the first animal looked like.</p>

<h2>What kinds of evidence tell the story?</h2>

<p>Comparative biology can take us only so far.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768598/original/file-20261027-92-hhblbt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Light circular fossil outline on surface of a tannish stone" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768598/original/file-20261027-92-hhblbt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768598/original/file-20261027-92-hhblbt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768598/original/file-20261027-92-hhblbt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768598/original/file-20261027-92-hhblbt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768598/original/file-20261027-92-hhblbt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768598/original/file-20261027-92-hhblbt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768598/original/file-20261027-92-hhblbt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Sometimes the remains of a living thing are transformed into stone – a fossil.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Dickinsonia_-_Ediacaran_Fossil_from_Flinders_Range_in_South_Australia.jpg">cprevot/Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Fossils are another source of information, but they show just a very narrow window into the past. <a href="https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/how-are-fossils-formed.html">Fossilization turns living material into stone</a>, a process that works far better on hard parts such as shells, teeth and bones than on soft, squishy bodies. Because early animals were probably soft and small, they were likely easily erased from the record.</p>

<p>Also, fossilization works better in some kinds of environments than others. For example, muddy lake bottoms can bury dead organisms, protecting their remains from rapid decay so they have time to fossilize; any remains on wave-battered shores may wash away before they can fossilize.</p>

<p>Another line of evidence now available to scientists is genetic information. Genes, encoded in DNA strands inside every living organism, provide an instruction manual for how to build that creature. Cells copy that DNA and pass it on – a process that’s been going on for billions of years, generation after generation.</p>

<p>This genetic information accumulates slight changes over time, which scientists call mutations. It is the very existence of mutations that allows evolution – how life changes over time – to happen. This process is <a href="https://evolution.berkeley.edu/evolution-101/an-introduction-to-evolution/">what generated the diversity of life</a> you see today.</p>

<p>By studying the structure and architecture of DNA, as well as how it gets passed along, scientists can mathematically assemble family trees that extend very deep into the past. These family trees can help scientists make surprisingly good guesses about when and where an animal first arose. A creature’s genes hint at what it could possibly do.</p>

<h2>Animals were assembled, not invented</h2>

<p>Biologist <a href="https://multicellgenome.com/">Iñaki Ruiz-Trillo</a> and his colleagues <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s44318-026-00692-5">use a smartphone analogy</a> that we find particularly useful when talking about the origin of animals.</p>

<p>A smartphone was not invented from scratch. Cameras, telephones, computers and the internet were all invented separately first. The innovation was combining them into a single piece of equipment.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770153/original/file-20261104-64-mwi37q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Hand with fine tool pokes at component of a deconstructed smartphone" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770153/original/file-20261104-64-mwi37q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770153/original/file-20261104-64-mwi37q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770153/original/file-20261104-64-mwi37q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770153/original/file-20261104-64-mwi37q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770153/original/file-20261104-64-mwi37q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770153/original/file-20261104-64-mwi37q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770153/original/file-20261104-64-mwi37q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The genius of a smartphone is that it brings several technologies together in one package.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/professional-repair-of-a-disassembled-smartphone-royalty-free-image/2162225288">Tetiana Strilchuk/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Animals may have evolved in a similar way. Genes for sticking cells together, for sending signals between cells, for sensing the environment and for switching other genes on and off were already present in our single-celled relatives. Becoming an animal meant assembling that tool kit into one cooperating body.</p>

<p>The first animal was probably something <a href="https://doi.org/10.1098/rsob.200359">very small, soft and unremarkable in an ancient ocean</a>. It probably evolved over 650 million years ago. It certainly had different kinds of cells that were stuck together, doing specialized jobs.</p>

<p>Scientists may never be able to pinpoint the first animal, and we have a hard time trying to imagine it. But we do know that many of the cellular and molecular tools that helped early animal cells work together are still at work in your body today.</p>

<title>A fungus that can survive in Chernobyl could help create materials that trap and break down nerve agents and pesticides</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772822/original/file-20261118-64-ychegm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5726%2C3817&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Scientists are researching fungi to develop specialized protective equipment for workers exposed to pesticides. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/male-asian-farmer-spray-fertilizer-at-tobacco-farm-royalty-free-image/1503208215?phrase=pesticides&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Vithun Khamsong/Moment via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Deep inside the Chernobyl exclusion zone, where radiation levels have remained unsafe for people for the past 40 years, <a href="https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20251125-the-mysterious-black-fungus-from-chernobyl-that-appears-to-eat-radiation">black molds climb the walls</a> of the damaged former nuclear plant in Ukraine. They’re entirely undeterred by the radiation – in fact, some fungi even grow toward it. </p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fmicb.2022.877625">The same type of species</a>, <em>Cladosporium sphaerospermum</em>, has grown on the International Space Station, about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above the surface of the Earth, in an experiment to test its resistance to radiation. Scientists found that it appeared to block a small amount of incoming radiation, and part of why comes down to a pigment called melanin.</p>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cladosporium_sphaerospermum#/media/File:Cladosporium_sphaerospermum_colony.jpg">Medmyco/Wikimedia Commons</a></span>

<p>I used to think of melanin the way most people do – as a pigment that gives skin, hair and eyes their color. That changed early <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=0JkUYOgAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">in my Ph.D. research</a> when I read <a href="https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.9b02160">a 2019 study</a> from the materials science lab I was joining that described how to make a fungal form of melanin in the lab. I was surprised by where this pigment shows up in nature, including in fungi growing at Chernobyl.</p>

<p>Melanin comprises a family of pigments. The melanin in human skin, called eumelanin, is built from nitrogen-containing building blocks. The melanin in many fungi, called allomelanin, is built from a different, nitrogen-free building block. That difference in structure gives it some unusual properties. </p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.0c12322">Scientists think allomelanin</a> is a large part of why these fungi can live in such places. Over the course of my doctoral research, I learned that melanin does much more than add color. It holds onto metals, absorbs ultraviolet light, converts light into heat and helps produce the colors of some bird feathers. </p>

<p>Allomelanin has another remarkable property. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.1c00748">My colleagues showed in 2021</a> that lab-made allomelanin is full of built-in pores, each less than a billionth of a meter wide. Chemists call these pores “intrinsic pores” because they are part of the material’s natural structure, rather than etched in later. To our knowledge, it is the only type of melanin with built-in porosity. </p>

<p>These nanometer-wide pores let the pigment act like a sponge for small molecules, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.1c00748">including toxic ones</a>, a feature we confirmed holds true whether the allomelanin comes directly from <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.ady4848">natural fungi or whether it is synthesized</a> in our lab.</p>

<p>In a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.6c06991">recent study published</a> in the peer-reviewed scientific journal ACS Nano, my colleagues and I asked whether this material could do more than trap toxic chemicals. Could it also break them down?</p>

<h2>Chemistry behind nerve agents and pesticides</h2>

<p>Nerve agents such as sarin and VX belong to a group of chemicals called <a href="https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Tsp/MMG/MMGDetails.aspx?mmgid=523&amp;toxid=93">organophosphorus compounds</a>. They <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK493158/">block an enzyme</a> the body uses to switch off nerve signals. Without that enzyme, nerves keep firing continuously, and a large enough exposure can turn lethal within minutes.</p>

<p>Chemical weapons are banned under international law, but they remain a persistent security concern. In May 2026, inspectors from the <a href="https://www.opcw.org/media-centre/news/2026/05/deployment-opcw-expert-team-syrian-arab-republic-finds-chemical-weapons">Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons reported</a> discovering dozens of previously undeclared chemical weapons in Syria left over from the Assad government.</p>

<p>Many pesticides used on agricultural crops rely on this exact same underlying chemistry. A <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1825899">2026 analysis estimated</a> that accidental pesticide poisonings number in the hundreds of millions each year, resulting in roughly 11,000 deaths annually around the world. Farmworkers operating with minimal protective gear face the greatest ongoing risk.</p>

<p>Today’s protective suits mostly rely on materials like activated carbon, which trap the chemicals but don’t break them down. Soldiers and farmworkers could benefit from protective gear that does more than block these toxic chemicals. Researchers, including my colleagues, are working on materials that could neutralize them as well. </p>

<h2>Adding a catalyst: Turning a sponge into scissors</h2>

<p>Allomelanin on its own holds on to these organophosphorus molecules but leaves them chemically intact. A contaminated glove or mask that has merely trapped these toxins would remain hazardous to handle.</p>

<p>To improve our sponge, my colleagues and I made allomelanin in the form of tiny spheres, each hundreds of times narrower than a human hair. We then added tiny clusters <a href="https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemmater.2c00262">made of a metal called zirconium</a>. Each cluster consists of six zirconium atoms anchored by oxygen – it looks like a tiny cage of zirconium held together by oxygen.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773136/original/file-20261119-62-5ww6ue.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Six slides showing microscopic images of a cluster of circular particles" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773136/original/file-20261119-62-5ww6ue.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773136/original/file-20261119-62-5ww6ue.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773136/original/file-20261119-62-5ww6ue.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773136/original/file-20261119-62-5ww6ue.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773136/original/file-20261119-62-5ww6ue.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773136/original/file-20261119-62-5ww6ue.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773136/original/file-20261119-62-5ww6ue.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Electron microscopy images of melanin nanoparticles loaded with zirconium clusters at increasing loadings. The nanoparticles keep their spherical shape at every loading. Their uniform spherical shape helps them disperse in solution and coat fabrics evenly, and their high surface area provides more active sites.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Sofia Aman</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Similar zirconium clusters form the active core of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat4238">metal-organic frameworks</a>, which are among the <a href="https://theconversation.com/metal-organic-frameworks-nobel-winning-tiny-sponge-crystals-with-an-astonishing-amount-of-inner-space-267089">most studied materials</a> for degrading chemical weapons. These clusters act like molecular scissors: When exposed to ambient moisture, they snip the chemical bonds holding organophosphates together, splitting them into less harmful pieces.</p>

<p>We tested different ways to attach these metal clusters to our synthetic allomelanin particles, ensuring the molecular scissors sat right where incoming toxins would land. </p>

<p>For safety, we tested the particles with a chemical stand-in widely used in research laboratories. It mimics nerve agents but carries far less toxicity. Our best-performing versions broke down half of the target chemical in less than 10 minutes, using only a tiny amount of zirconium. The particles kept working over several rounds of use, with very little metal leaking out.</p>

<p>Allomelanin’s built-in pores turned out to be essential. When we added the same zirconium clusters to other melanin-like materials without pores, they barely facilitated the breakdown. Adding too much zirconium also slowed the reaction, likely because more clusters clogged up the pores that water and toxic molecules needed to travel through. The best results came from balancing the amount of metal with open pore space.</p>

<h2>Using sunlight to power the cleanup</h2>

<p>This reaction usually needs <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/alkaline-condition">alkaline conditions</a>, which have a high pH and are the opposite of acidic – for example, baking soda dissolved in water is alkaline. </p>

<p>Water alone breaks down the trapped molecules far too slowly, over weeks or months. Alkaline conditions supply hydroxide, a negatively charged relative of water that is drawn to the molecule’s most dangerous bond and helps the zirconium snap it in minutes. In the lab, that means we add a liquid chemical to make the conditions alkaline, but doing so isn’t practical for a soldier’s jacket or a farmworker’s mask. Instead, we attached alkaline chemical groups directly to the particle surfaces.</p>

<p>We then took advantage of another property of melanin: It absorbs light and turns it into heat. Under a bright lamp for five minutes, the particles broke down about 10 times more of the stand-in chemical than they did in the dark. Simply heating the samples in the dark had a much smaller effect, which suggests light does more than warm the particles.</p>

<h2>What comes next</h2>

<p>Our work has important limits. We tested a chemical surrogate in laboratory vials rather than using live nerve agents or agricultural pesticides floating in the air. We also have not yet woven these particles into commercial textiles. Our immediate next steps are to evaluate the material against the specific pesticides farmworkers encounter daily and to refine the particle coating process.</p>

<p>Getting the material into fabrics may be more straightforward than it sounds. Synthetic melanin naturally adheres to textile fibers without needing chemical glues, and our research group <a href="https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.1c00748">has previously demonstrated</a> that synthetic melanins could act as sustainable fabric dyes. </p>

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Fabric with a specialized dye made from allomelanin applied.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Sofia Aman</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In the future, we hope this work can help develop lightweight gloves, masks and uniforms that continuously destroy toxic chemicals on contact as people work in the sun. Zirconium is a common and relatively inexpensive metal, and each particle uses only a small amount, though we haven’t evaluated what the cost of making these materials at a larger scale could be. </p>

<p>More broadly, this study highlights the untapped potential of natural materials. Fungi spent millions of years evolving pigments to endure some of the harshest environments on Earth. </p>

<p>I started my Ph.D. thinking of melanin simply as a biological colorant. I now see it as a versatile, multifunctional material whose full capabilities we are only beginning to unlock.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294087/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: The University of Florida revives the ‘Gator bait’ cheer, reversing a ban over its troubling history

<title>The University of Florida revives the ‘Gator bait’ cheer, reversing a ban over its troubling history</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771598/original/file-20261112-64-uh1yt9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=12%2C0%2C2879%2C1919&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The University of Florida&#39;s &quot;Gator bait&quot; chant has a complicated past.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/fan-of-the-florida-gators-holds-up-a-sign-that-reads-gator-news-photo/57059975?phrase=gator%20bait&amp;adppopup=true">Andy Lyons/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The sold-out crowd at <a href="https://floridagators.com/sports/2020/4/4/ben-hill-griffin-stadium">Ben Hill Griffin Stadium</a>, better known as “The Swamp,” roared with excitement as the University of Florida <a href="https://apnews.com/article/florida-gator-bait-cheer-returns-812f53da9a7a0d243d13d78f807b0b38">revived its “Gator bait” cheer</a> at its 2026 season opener. </p>

<p>When the marching band played the familiar cue, thousands of fans responded with the “Gator chomp,” raising their outstretched arms and repeatedly opening and closing their hands like alligator jaws while shouting “Gator bait!”</p>

<p>The decision to bring back the popular cheer <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2020/06/18/us/florida-gator-bait-spt-trnd">reversed a ban</a> imposed in 2020 by University of Florida President Kent Fuchs, who was concerned about its racist origins amid the nationwide <a href="https://www.npr.org/2020/08/16/902179773/summer-of-racial-reckoning-the-match-lit">reckoning over race</a> that followed the murder of George Floyd. </p>

<p>Current university president Stuart Bell remarked in an interview prior to his official appointment that “traditions matter” and suggested that the cheer could return because it <a href="https://247sports.com/college/florida/article/florida-athletics-president-finalist-dr-stuart-bell-gators-athletics-football-basketball-287501483/">remained “meaningful to the Gator family</a>.” Since then, the university has restored the cheer, though it has <a href="https://www.alligator.org/article/2026/09/gator-bait-cheer-returns-to-uf-football-games-after-6-years">not publicly identified who formally authorized its return</a>.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.alligator.org/article/2026/09/gator-bait-cheer-returns-to-uf-football-games-after-6-years">controversy surrounding this chant</a> has often been framed narrowly by its supporters as a dispute over tradition versus political correctness. However, it raises important questions about whether a public university should continue to <a href="https://www.alligator.org/article/2026/09/gator-bait-cheer-returns-to-uf-football-games-after-6-years">embrace a tradition</a> that <a href="https://www.tampabay.com/sports/gators/2020/09/02/how-the-great-grandson-of-a-slave-pushed-florida-to-end-gator-bait-cheer/">risks making some students and alumni</a> <a href="https://www.alligator.org/article/2020/06/gator-bait-chant-faced-opposition-years-ago-nothing-came-of-it">feel less welcome on campus</a>.</p>

<p>As an <a href="https://experts.vt.edu/2288-mark-barrow">environmental and cultural historian</a> and author of “<a href="https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/G/bo268426675.html">Gator!: The Making of America’s Iconic Reptile, from First Encounters to Florida Man</a>,” I’ve spent years researching how alligators became intertwined with ideas about race, nature and Southern identity. My research points to a deeper history largely absent from the public debate over the cheer.</p>

<h2>The making of ‘alligator bait’ as a racial slur</h2>

<p>The roots of the “alligator bait” trope stretch back to the 18th century, when French explorers in North America claimed that a “<a href="https://archive.org/details/newtravelsinnort0000boss/page/32/mode/2up">certain exhalation</a>” given off from Black skin attracted the voracious reptiles.</p>

<p>White plantation owners eagerly <a href="https://archive.org/details/beyondlinesoryan01geer/page/128/mode/2up">took up this racist theory</a> because it discouraged enslaved people from fleeing into Southern swamps and marshes, where pursuing runaways was often difficult.</p>

<p>After the Civil War, as formerly enslaved people sought economic, educational and political advancement, many white Americans responded with efforts to <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/575769/stony-the-road-by-henry-louis-gates-jr/">reassert white supremacy</a>. Alongside <a href="https://archive.org/details/shapingofsouther0000kous/mode/2up">disenfranchisement</a>, <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/606939833?oclcNum=606939833">Jim Crow segregation and racial terrorism</a>, they promoted <a href="https://www.upress.virginia.edu/title/1326/">stereotypes that demeaned and dehumanized African Americans</a>.</p>

<p>One of these racist stereotypes was the depiction of Black Americans, especially children, as natural prey for alligators. Though it operated through images and ideas rather than physical force, the stereotype reinforced beliefs in Black inferiority. It also helped justify the <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/i-saw-death-coming-9781635576634/">intimidation, exclusion and violence</a> that African Americans routinely faced during this period.</p>

<p>It was in this context that the racial slur “alligator bait” began circulating widely in the late 19th century. A <a href="https://www.icp.org/browse/archive/objects/alligator-bait">bestselling photograph</a> bearing that title, published in 1897, helped popularize the slur. Although the composite image of nine naked African American toddlers did not include an actual alligator, its title invited viewers to imagine Black children as special targets of the reptile.</p>

<p>The epithet soon spread through <a href="https://www.newspapers.com/image/1259629590/?match=1&amp;terms=%22alligator%20bait%22&amp;search-id=642dabed-15ad-4cb5-9fa3-4a311693c122&amp;search-rank=4">newspapers</a>, <a href="https://digitalcollections.nypl.org/items/b09dee30-2729-0132-45d3-58d385a7bbd0?canvasIndex=0">postcards</a>, <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alligator_bait#/media/File:Haiti_revolution_United_States_alligator_bait_editorial_cartoon.jpg">editorial cartoons</a>, <a href="https://levysheetmusic.mse.jhu.edu/collection/105/128">songs</a> and <a href="https://catalog.afi.com/Film/43108-ALLIGATOR-BAIT">films</a>. <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alligator_bait#/media/File:%22Fooled_dis_time,_Cully._Dis_cotton_aint_gwine_to_break%22._Merrick_Thread_Co._Best_Six_Cord_8_(front).jpg">Ostensibly humorous images</a> of alligators threatening or consuming Black Americans, especially children, also circulated widely across the U.S.</p>

<p>Whether Black children were ever actually used as bait to hunt alligators remains a subject of <a href="https://esnpc.blogspot.com/2020/04/live-human-alligator-bait-fact-or.html?m=1">historical debate</a>. But what is beyond dispute is that these images helped entrench degrading associations between African Americans and alligators in American popular culture for decades. </p>

<h2>‘Gator bait’ comes to campus</h2>

<p>As the phrase alligator bait gained currency across the United States, it also began appearing in a new setting: University of Florida football games. The earliest published reference to the cheer seems to be a <a href="https://www.newspapers.com/image/397814857/">1939 newspaper account</a> of a home game against Georgia Tech. </p>

<p>When Georgia Tech’s Yellow Jackets took the field, Florida students taunted the all-white team with cries of “alligator bait.” Georgia Tech’s coach used the insult to motivate his players, asking whether they could imagine “anything lower than that.”</p>

<p>While it is impossible to know precisely how everyone present understood the phrase, it entered Florida football culture at a time when “alligator bait” <a href="https://www.newspapers.com/image/1243037205/">remained a recognizable racial slur</a>. By the late 1940s, the shortened form, “Gator bait,” which was both easier to chant and more closely aligned with the university’s “Gators” nickname, had become a <a href="https://ufdc.ufl.edu/UF00028291/01401/images/9">regular fixture at Florida football games</a>.</p>

<p>The cheer remained firmly embedded in campus culture as the university navigated the slow and often contentious process of desegregation. <a href="https://floridapress.org/9780813034447/higher-education-and-the-civil-rights-movement/">Like most Southern universities</a>, the University of Florida resisted admitting Black students, <a href="https://access.heinonline.com/HOL/P?h=hein.journals/flsulr12&amp;i=69">enrolling its first African American law student</a>, George H. Starke, only after a court order in 1958. The first Black undergraduates arrived <a href="https://stars.library.ucf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=4563&amp;context=fhq">four years later</a>, and the football team <a href="https://stars.library.ucf.edu/fhq/vol88/iss4/4/">remained segregated until 1968</a>.</p>

<p>Desegregation did not immediately transform the broader campus culture. The university continued to embrace traditions that celebrated the Confederacy and romanticized the Old South. In 1962, football coach Ray Graves placed decals of the <a href="https://stars.library.ucf.edu/fhq/vol88/iss4/4/">Confederate battle flag</a> on his players’ helmets before the <a href="https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/bowls/gator-bowl.html">Gator Bowl</a>.</p>

<p>As late as the 1970s, the all-white Kappa Alpha fraternity continued a decades-long tradition of staging an annual <a href="https://www.newspapers.com/image/334886102/">“Old South” weekend</a> that featured students parading in Confederate uniforms. In the 1950s and 1960s, that celebration even included a <a href="https://www.newspapers.com/image/1260874418/">mock execution</a> of Union General William T. Sherman and a <a href="https://www.newspapers.com/image/334886102/">secession proclamation</a>. </p>

<p>When the <a href="https://ufdc.ufl.edu/UF00028291/02874/images/0">student newspaper surveyed the campus</a> in 1968 about whether to continue playing “Dixie” – the unofficial anthem of the Confederate States of America – at football games, 83% of students supported the practice. But the majority of Black students surveyed opposed it. “Dixie” remained a game-day staple <a href="https://stars.library.ucf.edu/fhq/vol88/iss4/4/">until 1973</a>.</p>

<h2>The many meanings of ‘Gator bait’</h2>

<p>By the late 20th century, most Florida fans no longer understood “Gator bait” through the lens of Jim Crow-era racial stereotypes. Decades of use at football games had transformed the chant into a symbol of school spirit and athletic success.</p>

<p>No individual played a larger role in that transformation than Lawrence Wright, the hard-hitting safety who helped lead Florida to its first national championship. Wright, who is African American, did not invent the cheer, as is <a href="https://www.alligator.org/article/2026/09/gator-bait-cheer-returns-to-uf-football-games-after-6-years">often claimed</a>, but he helped elevate it to iconic status. Following Florida’s victory over rival Florida State in 1995, he famously <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/1881140/2020/06/18/staples-gator-bait-and-the-collision-of-history-we-dont-know-with-history-we-do/">rallied fans with the refrain</a>, “If you ain’t a Gator, you must be Gator bait.” </p>

<p>When the Gators became <a href="https://floridagators.com/sports/2015/12/10/_football_history_php_his_ncaa1996_inc">national champions the next season</a>, the chant became even more deeply enshrined in Florida football culture. For most fans, “Gator bait” came to symbolize pride in the university rather than anything connected to the phrase’s earlier racist history.</p>

            </figcaption>

<h2>History clashes with the present</h2>

<p>Yet that history never disappeared.</p>

<p>While most fans were unaware of it, “alligator bait” <a href="https://archive.org/details/colorofwordsency0000herb/page/8/mode/1up">remained a documented racial slur</a>, creating a tension between the phrase’s historical origins and its modern meaning.</p>

<p>That tension came to a head in 2020, when Fuchs <a href="https://statements.ufl.edu/statements/2020/june/another-step-toward-positive-change-against-racism.html">suspended the cheer</a> amid a <a href="https://www.alligator.org/article/2020/07/students-continue-push-for-uf-administration-to-rename-campus-buildings">broader university effort to address racism</a> and inequity. While acknowledging that he knew of “no evidence of racism associated with our ‘Gator Bait’ cheer at UF sporting events,” Fuchs argued that the phrase’s “horrific historic racist imagery” warranted its retirement.</p>

<p>Critics, including Wright, responded that the cheer’s meaning at Florida had become <a href="https://www.gatorsports.com/football/20200618/lawrence-wright-disagrees-with-fuchs-decision-to-drop-gator-bait-cheer/">detached from those historical associations</a>. “Gator bait” was a cherished university tradition, <a href="https://www.reddit.com/r/FloridaGators/comments/hbhth5/university_athletics_and_the_gator_band_will/">they argued</a>, neither generally understood nor intended as racist.</p>

<p>Six years later, under Bell, the university has reinstated the cheer amid a <a href="https://www.npr.org/2024/03/04/1235725631/university-florida-cuts-dei-office">political and cultural climate markedly different</a> from the one that had prompted its suspension.</p>

<p>Still, I believe the <a href="https://www.wruf.com/headlines/2026/10/10/gator-bait-returns-but-not-all-agree-on-its-revival/">debate surrounding its return</a> reveals that the controversy has never simply been about political correctness or school spirit. In my view, it is also about how institutions reckon with difficult histories and whether traditions can be separated from the historical meanings that gave rise to them.</p>

<p>Even if most fans today understand the cheer as an expression of school spirit, universities do not simply inherit traditions. They choose which ones they wish to preserve, modify or discard.</p>

<p>Whether the university made the right decision is open to debate. What is not in dispute is that the “Gator bait” cheer emerged during a period when “alligator bait” functioned as a racial slur and the University of Florida excluded Black students while embracing traditions that celebrated the Confederacy.</p>

<p>The Conversation reached out to the university, and it declined to add to Bell’s previous comments on this matter.</p>

<title>Some people claim to speak many languages. But what does it really mean to be a polyglot?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773690/original/file-20261123-92-nnjjnj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C687%2C4126%2C2750&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Saying you can speak 20 languages doesn&#39;t necessarily mean you&#39;re fluent in all of them.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/illustration/languages-hand-drawn-vector-illustration-royalty-free-illustration/501441603?phrase=polyglot&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Sashatigar/iStock via Getty Images Plus </a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Roughly half of the world’s population <a href="https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003645412">speaks more</a> than one language. But speaking two or three languages is very different from claiming proficiency in five, 10 or more.</p>

<p>Throughout history, various people have attracted attention for their <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-52900-0_5">remarkable linguistic abilities</a>. Some have genuinely mastered numerous languages, while others have exaggerated their proficiency or struggled to demonstrate their purported abilities.</p>

<p>In my 2026 book “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009587389">Beyond Words: How We Learn, Use, and Lose Language</a>,” I explore the science of language, including how people acquire, understand and use it, from childhood language development to learning additional languages.</p>

<p>The word polyglot comes from the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/acref/9780198606536.001.0001">Greek word polyglōttos</a>, meaning “many-tongued.” It describes someone who speaks multiple languages, but it leaves some important questions unanswered: How many languages must someone know, and how proficient must they be, to earn the title?</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773122/original/file-20261119-62-xtj3pi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A woman wears headphones and stands next to a group of drawn flags of different countries." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773122/original/file-20261119-62-xtj3pi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773122/original/file-20261119-62-xtj3pi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=418&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773122/original/file-20261119-62-xtj3pi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=418&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773122/original/file-20261119-62-xtj3pi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=418&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773122/original/file-20261119-62-xtj3pi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=526&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773122/original/file-20261119-62-xtj3pi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=526&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773122/original/file-20261119-62-xtj3pi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=526&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The more languages someone claims to speak, the less likely they are to have a command of any language at all.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/young-woman-in-headphones-learning-different-royalty-free-image/1030492368?phrase=polyglot&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">SIphotography/iStock/Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Polyglots throughout time</h2>

<p>In the 1998 edition of the “Guinness Book of World Records,” Ziad Youssef Fazah was named the world’s <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-52900-0_5">greatest living polyglot</a>. Born in Liberia and raised speaking Arabic, Fazah claimed to speak, read and understand an astonishing 59 languages. At the time, <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1996/12/27/one-man-tower-of-babel/b8ff9082-d2c7-48db-8a6f-9911348db016/">The Washington Post dubbed him</a> the “One-man Tower of Babel.”</p>

<p>He was hardly the first person to attract attention for his supposed extraordinary linguistic abilities. </p>

<p>Cardinal Giuseppe Mezzofanti, an <a href="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20613094">Italian scholar</a> born in 1774, was reportedly proficient in 38 languages. </p>

<p>The <a href="https://doi.org/10.31430/QNME9229">10th-century philosopher</a> Al-Farabi was said to know 70 languages, while the 19th-century German linguist Hans Conon von der Gabelentz was <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/02549948.2025.2488686">believed to know 80 languages</a>, according to accounts of his linguistic abilities. Sir John Bowring, a British diplomat and governor of Hong Kong, <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/community.28212007.pdf">may have known</a> as many as 200 languages.</p>

<figure class="align-left zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773120/original/file-20261119-62-slyrh9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A black and white drawing of a man shows him seated in a formal, old fashioned suit." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773120/original/file-20261119-62-slyrh9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773120/original/file-20261119-62-slyrh9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=663&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773120/original/file-20261119-62-slyrh9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=663&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773120/original/file-20261119-62-slyrh9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=663&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773120/original/file-20261119-62-slyrh9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=833&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773120/original/file-20261119-62-slyrh9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=833&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773120/original/file-20261119-62-slyrh9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=833&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Such claims are difficult to verify, particularly when they concern historical figures. What counted as knowing a language? Was it familiarity with its vocabulary and grammar, the ability to read and write it, to translate, or to communicate comfortably with native speakers? These are very different levels of linguistic ability.</p>

<p>Fazah’s abilities were put to the test in 1997 on Chilean television. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-52900-0_5">During a live appearance</a>, he was asked basic questions in several languages, including Russian, Greek and Hindi. He struggled to answer correctly, even when asked relatively simple questions. The performance cast serious doubt on his claims, and his name subsequently disappeared from the “Guinness Book of World Records.” </p>

<p>The episode illustrates a crucial distinction: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0261444824000417">Knowing some of a language</a> is not the same as being fluent in it.</p>

<h2>What does it mean to speak a language?</h2>

<p>So, how fluent is fluent? </p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e37620">Fluency in a language is</a> not an all-or-nothing achievement. It is a spectrum, ranging from basic conversational ability to sophisticated, near-native command. Someone might understand a language quite well but struggle to speak it. Another person might hold a conversation comfortably but have difficulty reading or writing. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/applin/amp048">Proficiency can vary</a> across the different ways people understand and use a language.</p>

<p>Linguists generally assess <a href="https://doi.org/10.21832/9781788926317">language proficiency</a> across several areas, including speaking, listening, reading and writing. These abilities do not necessarily develop at the same rate. A person who can introduce themselves, order a meal and ask for directions may have a useful working knowledge of a language, but that is not the same as being able to debate politics, understand wordplay or conduct professional business in it.</p>

<p>This makes claims about polyglotism particularly difficult to evaluate. There is no simple threshold that determines when someone can legitimately say they <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/13621688211008693">speak a language</a>. And counting languages tells us little without knowing the level of proficiency in each.</p>

<h2>A genuine linguistic savant</h2>

<p>Not all extraordinary claims are exaggerated. </p>

<p>One remarkable example is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/9781119598732.ch23">Christopher Taylor</a>. A British savant who was born in 1960 and died in 2020, Taylor and his language abilities have long been studied by researchers. <a href="https://doi.org/10.5765/jkacap.230003">Savant syndrome</a> is a rare condition in which someone with a developmental or intellectual disability displays exceptional ability in a particular area, such as music, mathematics or, in Taylor’s case, languages.</p>

<p>Taylor experienced significant developmental delays as a child. As an adult he still required support with everyday activities. Yet he demonstrated an <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/9781119598732.ch23">extraordinary capacity</a> for learning languages. He could read, write, translate and converse in 15 to 20 languages, including Danish, Dutch, Finnish, German, Greek, Hindi, Italian, Norwegian, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Swedish, Turkish and Welsh.</p>

<p>His proficiency varied. In some languages he could hold a conversation; in others his understanding was more basic. But his ability to acquire <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0024-3841(91)90034-3">new linguistic knowledge</a> was remarkable. Much of his learning was self-directed, using introductory language books, dictionaries and interactions with native speakers.</p>

<p>In <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0024-3841(93)90002-E">one experiment</a>, published in 1993, Taylor learned the North African language Berber. Researchers found that he quickly grasped aspects of its complex grammar, including patterns of word order and verb agreement. He also mastered an artificial language called Epun, which researchers had invented specifically for the study. This suggested that his abilities extended beyond memorizing familiar words or phrases.</p>

<p>Taylor’s case is extraordinary, but it also offers a useful reminder: Even exceptional language ability comes in degrees. Researchers found that his proficiency varied considerably across languages. He was fluent in some, while in others he had only a basic knowledge. Being able to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263121000899">demonstrate knowledge</a> of a language in a controlled experiment is not necessarily the same as using it fluently in everyday life.</p>

<h2>How many languages can someone really learn?</h2>

<p>So is it possible to speak 20, 50 or even 100 languages? </p>

<p>Certainly, people can acquire knowledge of many languages, and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/cercor/bhaa205">some exceptional learners</a> can achieve impressive levels of proficiency across several. But the more languages someone says they speak, the more important it becomes to ask what that claim actually means.</p>

<p>Language is more than a collection of vocabulary and grammatical rules. It <a href="https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003160779">involves understanding</a> other people, responding spontaneously, interpreting cultural references and adapting to different social situations. A person may memorize thousands of words without being able to sustain a conversation. And proficiency is not necessarily permanent. Languages can become harder to use when they are not regularly practiced, particularly when someone is maintaining several at once.</p>

<p>Polyglots remind us of the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1515/9781614515173">remarkable flexibility</a> of the human mind. But their stories also challenge our assumptions about what it means to know a language. Rather than simply counting tongues, we need to look at what people can actually do with them.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/297026/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
