title: Why Trump saved Jensen Huang
excerpt: Donald Trump greets Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images This story appeared in&
body: Donald Trump greets Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is personally intervening to keep the AI industry afloat.  What happened? Jensen Huang, the recently ousted Nvidia CEO, is back atop the company as of Monday morning, after Trump dialed into an Nvidia board meeting over the weekend to offer “assurance” about legal and national security concerns around Huang.  Huang’s restoration — after he resigned following reports about multiple alleged affairs, including one with a possible Chinese spy — is a remarkable reversal of fortune
It also marks an unprecedented, at least in the modern era, level of direct White House interference with corporate America

What’s the context? This is the outcome that Trump, Elon Musk, and many of his other allies on the tech right have been agitating for since Huang stepped down not even two weeks ago.  As head of Nvidia, Huang has become — apparently quite literally — the AI industry’s “indispensable man.” In addition to being the leading maker of advanced AI chips, Nvidia is sometimes referred to as the “central bank of AI” for the financing schemes it uses to keep major labs afloat
That gives it a great deal of sway over better-known companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.  Huang, by some in the industry and on Wall Street, was considered central to those efforts

Markets jumped dramatically Monday morning on news of his return.  Why does this matter? His return is a boon for the stock market and the AI industry just as both were starting to stumble, and one that may temporarily fend off the “perfect storm” that my colleague Eric Levitz described last week

It’s also an exceptional moment of naked self-interest by Trump, choosing the market’s continued well-being and his personal friendship with Huang over real national security concerns about Huang’s leadership at Nvidia.  What now? The Huang scandal won’t end here
He’s set to testify in the Senate next Thursday, and that’s likely just the start of the congressional oversight he can expect with incoming Democratic majorities in both chambers
After today, where that will lead is anyone’s guess

And with that, it’s time to log off… Hi readers, happy Thanksgiving week! If you’re getting ready to travel for the holiday, Vox’s Unexplainable podcast just tackled one of the most pressing questions out there: Should you recline your seat on a plane?  In typically excellent Unexplainable fashion, they consulted science and moral philosophy to find the answer, with some help from the New Yorker’s Joshua Rothman
Have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!

title: Can the Nvidia scandal possibly get weirder?
excerpt: President Donald Trump presents the National Medal of Science to Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, at an October 2026 event in Washington, DC. | Kent Nishimura/AFP v
body: President Donald Trump presents the National Medal of Science to Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, at an October 2026 event in Washington, DC. | Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
It is truly wild that an executive with several reported affairs, a reputation for violently berating his staff, and a trail of deeply questionable deals could be invited back for a second go-round

Then again, if President Donald Trump managed it…then why not his buddy, Jensen Huang? Huang, the ex-ex-Nvidia CEO, is officially back at the helm of the giant chipmaker he cofounded 35 years ago — and all his past indiscretions have been forgiven, if still under investigation
And the stock market loves it , with investors joining Trump in betting that Huang’s singular business talents will make up for the considerable chaos he’s personally caused already
Huang, you’ll recall, resigned less than two weeks ago following reports that he’d had an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China
Whether she actually was a spy is still an open question
But other reporting has since cast lots of doubts on different aspects of Huang’s conduct and character
Like: reports that Nvidia, under Huang’s watch, may have indirectly sold restricted chips to China

Or that Huang allegedly told an employee he’d rip off his head and “pee on [his] brain,” among a number of other, er…inventive humiliations.  And yet! On Sunday, Nvidia’s board voted unanimously to reinstate him, apparently at the request of Trump himself. “I spoke to them
And I convinced them,” Trump told CNBC in a Monday morning segment

Key to that decision: The president’s personal assurance that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” It’s an extraordinary turn in an extraordinary story that we very likely have not seen the end of just yet
Because the fight over Huang is also a fight over how America can continue dominating the high-stakes field of artificial intelligence
Go a little deeper View Link Before the scandal, before the spying allegations, before all the drama…Huang was already a central player in the bitter debate over selling AI chips to China
The US restricts sales of some kinds of cutting-edge chips for fear they could help China develop more advanced AI

Huang has spent months telling Trump he should loosen those restrictions. (It’s not particularly difficult to imagine why.) But as my colleague Andrew Prokop breaks down today , lawmakers, AI executives, and officials within Trump’s own administration are not sold

In fact, they’re deeply divided over whether loosening sales restrictions on AI chips would ultimately advance or erode America’s AI dominance.  In one camp are the so-called “China hawks,” who argue that selling powerful chips to China would very likely accelerate its AI development at America’s expense
In the other camp are Nvidia and its allies in Trump’s orbit

They argue that America is better off selling China  some chips — and keeping Chinese developers dependent on American technology — than abandoning that market to the Chinese competition.  This divide  doesn’t map neatly onto party lines

While most prominent Democrats fall toward the hawkish end of the spectrum, the China question has divided Trump’s coalition.  Many GOP lawmakers and some of Trump’s top officials — including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent — side more or less with Democrats on this

So does much of the national security establishment and the AI safety movement.   Meanwhile, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and former White House AI adviser David Sacks have made the case for keeping Chinese developers hooked on American chips
And Trump has increasingly favored their approach, growing generally more conciliatory toward China since his first term

Last year, his administration loosened restrictions on some Nvidia chip sales to China . (And last week Trump was, for what it’s worth , photographed holding Xi Jinping’s hand on an escalator.) But Huang’s return won’t settle the China AI argument for long, regardless of Trump’s influence
When Democrats take control of Congress in January, they’ll gain the power to launch more rigorous investigations — including into Nvidia
And at least a few Republicans also say they have questions.  “Who in our government weighed in?” asked Sen

John Curtis (R-UT) in a post on X , referring to Huang’s reinstatement. “What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?” One link for later ➨ Indulge your inner child
In the US, adults without kids now officially buy more toys than adults with children

That fact initially struck me as odd, but… there’s a neurological justification ! When people of any age play with toys, the part of the brain that governs the stress response calms down. “The drive to play is actually biologically hardwired into our subcortex,” one expert told Vox
Before you go… Did you know …that female turkeys can basically clone themselves ? Occasionally, the eggs of female turkeys will spontaneously develop into embryos without any sperm
Today’s trivia: Which 19th-century author and activist is known as “the mother of Black feminism”? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Last week we asked you for the name of the independent federal agency currently chaired by Kevin Warsh
That would be the Federal Reserve System — a.k.a. the Federal Reserve or the Fed — which sets monetary policy in the US.

title: Jensen Huang’s return proves Trump and the tech right still call the shots
excerpt: A television broadcasts Nvidia news on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) on November 23, 2026. | Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty For a brief mom
body: A television broadcasts Nvidia news on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) on November 23, 2026. | Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty For a brief moment after the 2026 midterms, it had seemed that President Donald Trump was a true lame duck already
First came Democrats’ blue tsunami, a popular rejection of his record by voters that threatens to constrain much of his agenda

Then there was the ouster of Jensen Huang , a celebrity CEO who had been deeply influential on the Trump administration’s AI and chip policy, to bipartisan chagrin , and was arguably the single most important private individual in the broader economy .  Huang’s downfall came after allegations that he had affairs with two employees as well as a tech executive who some US officials thought was a Chinese spy

And it seemed to signify that the era in which Trump and the tech right — a group of wealthy venture capitalists and CEOs who backed Trump, such as Elon Musk and David Sacks — ran the country was over
Just 11 days after Huang resigned, Nvidia made the shocking announcement Monday that it was putting him back in the CEO job
And the company did so after a very public campaign from leading tech right figures and Trump

The president reportedly called into Nvidia’s board meeting as the company weighed Huang’s return, and in a CNBC interview Monday, Trump referred to the outcome as a “deal” that he’d made. “I spoke to them

And I convinced them,” he said .  In their own announcement, Nvidia indicated that the White House assured them Huang was not a security liability, even as the company said it would continue its own internal investigation

Trump quickly confirmed that these assurances came from the very top. “The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security,” Trump posted on Truth Social . “The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S
Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” “On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure,” Trump added

Meanwhile, tech investors aligned with Trump popped the champagne as soon as the news broke. “The mistake,” Musk tweeted , “has been corrected.” It’s an astonishing sequence of events — and a flex of power by the president and the tech right
Trump personally intervened to ensure one of the biggest companies in the world would once again be led by an executive embroiled in a personal misconduct and national security scandal
In the CNBC interview Monday, Trump dismissed the national security concerns in a rather odd way

He said that, in fact, ousting Huang as CEO would be worse for national security, because Xi Jinping might lure him over to lead a Chinese company, and Huang may have done it out of anger because he has “a little blood in him.”  At least part of Trump’s motivation may have been the headwinds facing the tech-and-AI-powered stock market in recent weeks, including a brutal day of declines on Friday that led many to question whether a bubble had finally popped
If Trump’s goal was to juice the markets, it worked — at least for now
Indeed, in the first minute after trading opened, the value of Nvidia increased about 33 percent
That’s $1 trillion in value that, in the minds of investors, would not have existed if not for Huang’s return

But Huang’s restoration amidst scandal also seemed to epitomize the philosophy Trump had once infamously expressed, in a very different context : “I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody, and I wouldn’t lose any voters, okay?” It’s a massive test of whether Trump’s ability to survive scandal after scandal on the basis of charisma and political hardball is transferable to someone else, even a CEO who has drawn his company into an international crisis with his personal behavior.  All this seemed exemplified in a bizarre Truth Social post from Trump Monday morning : an AI-generated image re-creating the famed photo of Trump rising bloodied after his 2024 assassination attempt — only with Huang in Trump’s place, a flag with Nvidia’s logo flying, and Huang raising a red bra

From our President and Nvidia’s 12th board member (yes, this is a real post) pic.twitter.com/PgXo9nMlaN — Rohan Goswami (@rogoswami) November 23, 2026 But can it last? Huang’s return is an incredible display of resilience — for now

He still has his many enemies in Washington, among both political parties, some of whom are already warning him and his backers not to get too comfortable.  Those problems start with the incoming Democrats in Congress, who will soon have subpoena power in both the House of Representatives and the Senate — and who will now be more motivated than ever to investigate this topic

Even before they take over, Huang is set to testify before the Senate, as is Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , the Cabinet official most closely associated with the pro-Huang bloc and whose dovish approach to Chinese chips has come under bipartisan fire. “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” Sen
Chuck Schumer (D-NY) — in the midst of a contested bid to regain his old post as majority leader — posted on X

Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), in line to chair the Senate Banking Committee, posted that the decision to reinstate Huang was “reckless,” adding : “The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement.” But this issue is not confined to Trump’s partisan opponents either

Pete Ricketts (R-NE), freshly reelected to a new six-year term, warned on Monday that the decision “doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns” and strongly criticized Huang’s behavior. “I’ve served on a public company board,” he wrote on X. “His behavior does not support reinstatement.” Sen

John Curtis (R-UT), meanwhile, wanted to know more about the Trump administration’s involvement. “Who in our government weighed in?” Curtis posted . “What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?” Sen

Kevin Cramer (R-ND) went even further, asserting that Huang “may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws,” and saying his rehiring caused a serious “national security risk.” Indeed, there’s significant Republican antipathy toward Huang as well among “China hawks,” who have long viewed Huang’s enthusiasm for selling Nvidia’s chips abroad — including, in the case of certain chips, to China — as harmful to American national security and the US’s place at the front of the AI race.  They were sharply critical of Huang well before news broke of Huang’s affair with a purported spy. “China hawks are patient and have long memories,” former congressional defense policy aide Eric Sayers wrote in criticism of Huang last year, and repeated as the Huang scandals were emerging

These hawks include longtime members of Washington’s national security establishment and many GOP senators and members of Congress, as well as some of Trump’s own top officials — like Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent

Days after Huang’s ouster, the hawks seemed newly empowered, as the Trump administration issued a rule to crack down on chip sales abroad and Chinese remote access to American AI technology — a policy Huang’s allies in the administration had previously resisted
Bessent in particular had seemed triumphant after Huang’s downfall

Last week, he said on Fox Business that the company needed “a dramatic shake-up” and that, “as the board conducts a search for a new leader, they need to go outside the company.” But after Trump started to champion Huang’s return, Bessent changed his tune , attempting to argue that Huang’s restoration would meet his standard because “Jensen is on the outside now.” Huang’s enemies will be watching him — and Nvidia and the White House — like a hawk for any sign of deference to China or for new information that might put Huang’s leadership role back into question

And with corruption emerging as a major political liability for both Trump and his party, any suspected signs of favor-trading or profiteering — Huang’s $25 million donation to the presidential ballroom has already drawn attention, as well as Trump’s multimillion-dollar Nvidia trades — will face intense scrutiny as well, especially from newly empowered Democratic legislators. “The President is selling out our national security to keep the stock market high and probably for some fucking donation to his ballroom,” Sen
Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) posted on X on Monday For now, though, these critics’ attacks and concerns have all been swept away
Trump remains the most powerful man in the country — and often, he can still get his way
Update, November 23, 2026, 2:55 pm ET: This post was originally published midday Monday
It has been updated to include more statements from senators.

title: Democrats’ tantalizing dream of a Blue Utah
excerpt: An American flag hangs in Orem, Utah, while the Orem Utah Temple of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints rises in the background. | Charles-McClintoc
body: An American flag hangs in Orem, Utah, while the Orem Utah Temple of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints rises in the background. | Charles-McClintock Wilson/Getty Images If someone asked which shift or flip was most surprising in this year’s blue tsunami, you might be hard-pressed to choose
Kansas elected its first Democratic senator in nearly a century
Republicans lost every statewide race in Texas
With Democrats winning in South Carolina and Mississippi, conventional wisdom about what counts as a battleground went completely out the window
A state that last voted for a Democratic presidential candidate in 1964; a bastion of cultural conservatism and business-friendly politics; the home of Mitt Romney and the Mormon church
And now…although a handful of votes are still waiting to be counted, it looks like, for the first time in decades, more votes were cast for Democrats than Republicans in Utah this cycle

Is this just another high spot for a fluke blue wave — or a pivot in American political history? For Democrats, the results have led to some improbable dreams about “Blutah,” a middle-of-the-nation state that, like Colorado, could be swinging from a GOP stronghold into a Democratic opportunity
It’s not yet clear how likely that is; there was no galvanizing statewide race on the Utah ballot this year, and registered Republicans still dramatically outnumber Democrats
The 2026 results could just be a phenomenon of a blue-wave midterm year, where the absence of a presidential contest left more Republican-friendly voters at home
But the Utah results didn’t come out of nowhere

There have been signs throughout the last decade of simmering discontent with the Trump-era Republican Party — some of which are specific to Utah, and some of which connect to trends that extend far beyond its borders
What happened in the midterms may be a preview of a future political coalition that was hard to imagine at the start of the Trump era

The state as a whole has changed dramatically in the last 15 years, experiencing a population boom , racial diversification , and an influx of both wealthier, college-educated residents as well as those looking for a more affordable state in which to live

At the same time, the makeup and ideological views of Mormons — members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, the state’s most influential institution — have also changed during the Trump era

Those two shifting electorates foreshadow both a reordering of state politics and a broader trend in American society: that youth, racial diversity, and secularization may continue to turn uncontested or unchanging territory into competitive battlegrounds in the future
MAGA and Mormonism have never fully gotten along It’s impossible to talk about Utah politics without talking about Mormons, the most influential segment of the Utah electorate
Though their share of the state population has declined over the last decade, they still make up anywhere from 40 percent to 60 percent of the state, depending on how you measure Mormon identity
Nationally, Mormons make up about 2 percent of the population, one of the five largest Christian denominations in the US
And they’ve tended to back Republicans by lopsided margins that rival only white evangelical Christians
Despite their conservative streak and history, Mormons have had an uneasy relationship with the MAGA-era GOP, and the results suggest that may now be getting worse

Though officially nonpartisan, Mormon leaders have pushed for social justice initiatives that contrast with the Trump agenda, and were early critics of the president’s immigration campaign promises back in 2016 (when a Church-backed newspaper called on President Donald Trump to leave the race after the Access Hollywood scandal)
Some have questioned his commitment to conservative social politics
The most prominent Mormons involved in politics — Romney, Gov
Spencer Cox, independent Evan McMullin, and current Sen
John Curtis — have staked out territory as Trump skeptics or antidotes

Though it seems long ago, Trump came in last place during the state’s 2016 Republican presidential primary, winning just 14 percent of the vote, while McMullin ran as an independent during the general election and siphoned votes from Trump
Trump support has remained very soft in Utah
And those tensions bubbled to the surface again in 2022, when Sen
Mike Lee faced a surprisingly competitive challenge from McMullin

Romney, at the time Lee’s Republican colleague in the Senate, pointedly refused to endorse him, while church leadership was reportedly frustrated with Lee’s MAGA turn. (Lee’s coming reelection fight may turn out to be the next big test of “Blutah.”) Beyond the personal gripes Mormon voters and leaders may have had with Trump, their alienation from the Trump-era GOP has some deeper causes
Immigration politics have always been a sticking point for this global church

Young Mormons famously must go on evangelizing missions as part of their faith formation; those assignments place them in diverse and heterogeneous places, especially abroad, and color the experiences of older church and political leaders
The church has expanded rapidly outside of the US, with new temples being constructed in Africa and Latin America
The anti-immigrant turn of the Trump-era GOP fits poorly with this cosmopolitan worldview
Church leadership has spent the last decade projecting a moderate voice on immigration while trying not to antagonize the administration, occasionally speaking about enforcement policies domestically

That mismatch doesn’t necessarily make Mormons into natural Democrats, but it does make them a bad fit for MAGA Republicanism.  The post-pandemic GOP’s embrace of Christian nationalist rhetoric and ideology has also tested its bonds with Mormonism
In June, Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon temporarily branded Mormonism a non-Christian religion

The attacks by various segments of MAGA on Muslims and Jews, and the broader movement on the right to chip away at the separation of church and state , all sit badly with a church whose own roots are in a refugee community that suffered official persecution. “LDS members are very sensitive to attacks on religious minorities because they themselves are a religious minority,” Dave Campbell, a longtime religion and politics scholar at the University of Notre Dame and expert in Mormon politics, told me. “They see themselves as under attack when they hear other minority religions being attacked.” The Mormon electorate is changing, too The religious, social, and cultural differences between the church and MAGA are also being driven by a broader generational divide between younger LDS members and older ones, Campbell told me
Younger LDS voters are simply less likely to identify with the GOP, vote for Republican candidates, agree with the church’s conservative social teachings, and be personally devout, he said

They are more racially diverse, are more comfortable with same-sex relationships, and less strict on abortion politics, Campbell said. “These are young people who are generally more liberal, not just religiously, but also politically,” Campbell told me

title: How to talk to kids, according to kids
excerpt: Nine-year-old Leo is attempting to share his screen with me over FaceTime for a very important reason: I must hear an extremely funny sound — the clang of a met
body: Nine-year-old Leo is attempting to share his screen with me over FaceTime for a very important reason: I must hear an extremely funny sound — the clang of a metal pipe hitting the ground
The mere act of pulling up the YouTube video causes our call to glitch and we’re forced to reconnect
With the technical difficulties sorted, I do admit the sound is funny in an exaggerated, cartoonish way
But why does this crash in particular, this specific clip, tickle his funny bone? “Because if it annoys mommy enough, it’s funny,” Leo told me
This conversation with Leo was one of several I had recently with kids between the ages of 6 and 11 where I asked them on how they like to have fun and with whom
I don’t consider myself adept at making small talk with anyone under the age of 20, mainly because I’m hardly around any such people
Most of my friends don’t have little ones and at family parties, I smile politely at my cousins’ kids from afar
My attempts at conversation with the youth feel strained and awkward opposed to snappy and light, so I figured this assignment would be good practice
Chances are, you know some kids — a friend’s toddler, a relative’s tween — and might need a little guidance, too

When I asked Leo whether the adults in his life could be better at interacting with children, he cut me off. “This adult particularly?” he said, gesturing to his mother, just off camera. “No, she is perfect

Other adults in general, maybe.” As more adults choose not to have kids , or wait later in life to do so , it’s entirely possible you, like me, don’t spend a ton of time with small humans and can’t remember what it was like to be one

What do they even like? How do you keep their attention? How do you avoid saying the wrong thing? Figuring this out is important given that intergenerational relationships are a net positive for both adults and kids : Grown-ups get the chance to learn from the young people in their lives and, in turn, children soak in older generations’ knowledge and wisdom
Plus, if most of us agree “it takes a village” when it comes to raising kids, it’s worth trying to be good villagers.  So I decided to ask the experts: Kids themselves
From my conversations, I’ve distilled a few do’s and don’ts for how to have better conversations with kids

Find some common ground (animals are a safe bet) In nearly every one of my conversations, children mentioned caring about, thinking about, or being interested in, animals. “If [grown-ups] just want to be my friend, maybe they could introduce them[selves] to me and tell [me] what their favorite animal is, and then maybe I’ll get used to them and then I start liking them better,” Logan, 9, told me
Kids seem especially primed to enjoy wildlife
In one study, when children were presented with the option of interacting with toys or animals, they consistently chose animals

Animals are varied and visually engaging , giving kids plenty to be fascinated with.  Logan and her 6-year-old sister Apple play a 20 questions-style game called “guess the animal.” The trickiest animal she’s offered clues for was a gila monster. “It’s kind of like a lizard and it’s flat
It’s like a reptile and it’s orange and black,” Logan said
Even if you don’t have a lot to say in the creature department, try to find some commonality
The key is to pay attention to what kids seem genuinely curious about and to invite them into your world — or to try to get an invite to theirs
Eleven-year-old Eli’s interests range from history and war reenactments to Legos and Call of Duty

Some of the adults in his life leveraged these subject areas and have found common ground: He connects with his uncle over a shared love of outdoorsy adventures, and a few neighbors over their historic cars and the military
Do an activity together  It should come as no surprise that kids like to do stuff, as opposed to boring adults who mostly like to talk

Seven-year-old Winona introduced herself as “a kid with a lot of energy,” which means she loves to play tag and hide-and-seek — an activity one of her aunts is happy to partake in whenever she visits. “If I had a world and it was called Winnieland, every adult would play with me,” Winona told me. “We would ride roller coasters

And what’s my favorite thing? My favorite thing is, oh, I know: obstacle courses and haunted houses.” Leo, too, thinks it’s easier to connect with adults when you’re doing something together, like playing a video game
His tia is one of the best Mario Kart players he’s ever seen.  Nothing lights up 8-year-old Hugo quite like soccer

I sensed some initial hesitation when we spoke, but any time our meandering chat came back to the sport, he suddenly had much more to say. (He’s on three teams, according to his mom.) Kicking around a ball is a great way to bond with him
Adults could be more interesting to kids, Hugo said, if they didn’t work so much, if they didn’t have so much to do. “My friends are always active, and my parents are always doing stuff,” he said
Activity-based bonding, like singing, telling stories, and reading to children, promotes positive social-emotional development in kids , according to research
Families with school-aged kids who engage in physical activity together had improved cohesion, per another study

Doing an activity or playing a game removes the pressure to keep the conversation going — you can simply talk about the thing in front of you, and it’s okay to sit in silence for a couple minutes while you color if you can’t think of anything to say.  Get a little playful Aside from her parents, a few of Logan’s favorite adults to interact with are her teacher and teacher’s assistant
What makes her TA especially skilled at connecting with children is her ability to imagine and play, Logan said
One day at recess, Logan and a friend took turns trying on the TA’s lanyard, pretending they were in charge
Rather than shut them down, the TA upped the ante: “She said that she was going to steal the principal’s name tag and say that she was the principal,” Logan said
Logan’s preferred form of play involves dreaming up new universes and games and when grown-ups can join in and play pretend, all the better
Getting on kids’ wavelength might mean suspending disbelief, too
Winona told me that when she was younger, she had an imaginary friend named Christopher, a raccoon who was prone to making a mess
If connecting with a kid means referring to a fake racoon by name, it’s a conversational path worth taking
All the kids I talked to seemed to notice and appreciate when adults are down to play — when they don’t rationalize make-believe scenarios and logic, and instead lean into silliness

title: The Supreme Court is about to decide whether to gut countless federal laws
excerpt: Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch, left, and Chief Justice John Roberts on the steps of the Supreme Court in 2017 in Washington, DC. | Win McNamee/Getty Images
body: Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch, left, and Chief Justice John Roberts on the steps of the Supreme Court in 2017 in Washington, DC. | Win McNamee/Getty Images Nearly five decades ago, in Cannon v

Chicago (1979), the Supreme Court held that Title IX, the federal law forbidding most schools from engaging in sex discrimination, could be enforced by private plaintiffs filing individual lawsuits against those schools
It was an important decision, because without it, Title IX would be a much weaker law that would only function when the federal government charges someone with violating it
The Court has since reaffirmed its decision in Cannon at least four times , provided that the plaintiff alleges intentional discrimination
And yet, on November 30, the Supreme Court will hear Crowther v

Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia , a case that asks whether Title IX’s prohibition on sex discrimination may be enforced by through such individual lawsuits.  The fact that this Court took up a legal question that the Supreme Court has already answered many times is an ominous sign for victims of sex discrimination — and potentially for millions of other individuals whose rights to education, healthcare, and numerous other essentials are protected by federal law

The best case scenario for civil rights plaintiffs is that the justices simply hand down a sixth decision reaffirming a longstanding right, and the worst case scenario could render countless federal laws unenforceable

Crowther involves a highly technical, but extremely important legal concept known as “ implied causes of action .” Not all federal laws may be enforced by private litigants in court — sometimes, for example, only the federal government itself is allowed to sue in order to enforce a particular law
Some statutes, meanwhile, contain an explicit provision stating that private individuals may bring lawsuits to enforce them.  Other laws, including Title IX, do not explicitly authorize suits

But the Supreme Court nonetheless concluded in Cannon and in several other decisions that a right to sue is implicit in Title IX’s text — that is, it contains an “implied cause of action.” Until recently, the Court’s decision in Gonzaga University v

Doe (2002) laid out the rules that judges were supposed to use in order to determine whether a particular federal law contains an implied cause of action, and therefore may be enforced by private plaintiffs
But the rules governing implied causes of action grew muddled a little over a year ago, when the Court’s decision in Medina v
Planned Parenthood (2025) seemed to abandon Gonzaga
They grew even more muddled in June, when the Court handed down yet another decision reaffirming Gonzaga
So it’s now impossible even for veteran civil rights lawyers to determine which laws may be enforced through individual lawsuits
In any event, Crowther gives the Court a prime opportunity to resolve this confusion, and clarify which laws may actually be enforced by private litigants
The stakes in this case, moreover, are absolutely enormous, as a too-stingy approach to implied causes of action would deactivate a wide array of federal laws
Many of the Court’s most important implied causes of action cases, for example, involve Medicaid — a federal program that provides health c are to nearly 73 million people

If federal Medicaid law — which doesn’t just provide health coverage to low-income patients but also lays out a long list of rights those patients enjoy — becomes unenforceable, millions of lives will be jeopardized
These cases often go to the heart of Americans’ ability to care for themselves and their loved ones
Talevski (2023), the Court held (among other things) that a federal law that prohibits nursing homes from unnecessarily drugging their patients into a stupor is enforceable
In Medina , the Republican justices effectively repealed a federal law that allows Medicaid patients to choose their own health provider

Crowther , in other words, could be one of the most consequential — and one of the cruelest — decisions the Court hands down during its current term, because a decision for the defendants in Crowther could effectively turn countless lifesaving federal laws into a nullity
What are the rules governing implied causes of action? One frustrating thing about this area of the law is that the justices frequently change the rules governing implied causes of action

In the 1960s the Court took an expansive approach to implied causes of action , but it spent much of the later two decades of the 20th century limiting which federal laws may be enforced by private lawsuits

Still, this area of the law appeared to stabilize when the Court handed down Gonzaga , which held that “for a statute to create private rights [to sue], its text must be phrased in terms of the persons benefited .” Thus, for example, if Congress passes a law stating that “no dirty person shall be denied access to a bath,” this law would be enforceable through private lawsuits because the law is phrased in terms of who benefits from it (dirty people)

A similar federal law which says that “states may not impede access to bathing facilities” would be unforceable by private litigants, because this hypothetical law lacks the person-focused language required by Gonzaga
If Gonzaga is still good law, then Crowther is an open and shut case

Here is the relevant language from Title IX : No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance Like the hypothetical law allowing dirty people to bathe, Title IX opens by stating who the law is intended to benefit (“no person in the United States”)
So, under Gonzaga , Title IX may be enforced by private plaintiffs in federal court

Indeed, Gonzaga even named Title IX as an example of a law that may be enforced by private litigants because it is “ phrased ‘with an unmistakable focus on the benefited class .’” But then Medina threw the rules governing implied causes of action into bedlam

Justice Neil Gorsuch’s majority opinion in Medina neither applies the Gonzaga rule nor quotes its most important language — the line about statutes being “phrased in terms of the persons benefitted.” But it also doesn’t explicitly overrule Gonzaga
Medina says that laws that impose obligations on institutions that accept federal funding, such as Title IX or Medicaid, are particularly unlikely to be enforceable by private litigants
But it never lays out a legal rule that judges can use to determine which of these sorts of laws are enforceable in court

Some of Gorsuch’s opinion indicates that a statute may be enforceable if it uses the magic word “right,” but his opinion never explains whether statutes that don’t use this particular word can nonetheless be enforced by private litigants
One likely explanation for this confusing decision is that Medina was merely a cynical attempt to spite an abortion provider
The specific legal question in Medina was whether a federal law that allowed Medicaid patients to choose their health provider allowed them to choose Planned Parenthood
If the Court had applied Gonzaga in this case, Planned Parenthood would have won
So the Court’s Republicans most likely joined Gorsuch’s incomprehensible decision because they wanted to ensure that Planned Parenthood would lose

Yet, regardless of why the Court decided to unsettle such an important area of the law in Medina , the fact remains that Medina transformed the rules governing implied causes of action into an unfathomable mess

title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
excerpt: AI keeps getting faster at verifiable tasks — METR's updated report confirms that frontier AI models are doubling their performance on measurable tasks eve
body: AI keeps getting faster at verifiable tasks — METR's updated report confirms that frontier AI models are doubling their performance on measurable tasks every four months
Judgment is where models still stumble — When asked to design new AI evaluations or score philosophical arguments, even the most advanced models fell short of human performance

Some glimmers of progress, but no clean trend lines — A handful of newer models are now scoring "borderline above the bar" on evaluation design tasks, up from "clearly below" just a year ago — though researchers warn these improvements are too sparse to predict where things are headed. " data-chronoton-post-id="1149399" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding
The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used
METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans
Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete
That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled
The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended

One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure

We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures
That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work
It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction
For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them
But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development
And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now

Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two

That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement
METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development
In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results

Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research
In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments
This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D
On this task, too, models fell short of human performance

Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.” Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August , he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own

And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite
Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says

Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well

And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.  Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better
Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR’s research, but promising
Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category

But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.” Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].” In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D

METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.  In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming

Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual
It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming
It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment

And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says
But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”

just a year ago — though researchers warn these improvements are too sparse to predict where things are headed.

title: The Download: inside the quest to make our minds immortal
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
What we learned when our Roundtables explored the quest to make minds immortal To preserve our sense of self, some scientists are working on ways to keep our brains going—even beyond death
In their quest for cognitive immortality, these “mind savers” are exploring everything from head transplants and brain freezing to conscious software avatars
In the latest MIT Technology Review Roundtables event, senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado joined science editor Mary Beth Griggs to examine these ideas
After following the money, the science, and the philosophy, he came back part skeptical, part awestruck
Here’s a taste of what Antonio found—and what he made of it

Not all the projects are quite what they seem: A $190 million US government program to develop replacement brain tissue is officially about treating stroke, but “it’s also a fig leaf for the actual ambition”: living forever

AI could lead to convincing mind clones: Large language models are making it possible to build AI copies of people that act quite like the real thing. “This digital avatar might not be good enough for you, but what if it’s good enough for me?” Immortality can be a hard sell: One company, Nectome, wants to preserve brains within 12 minutes of medically assisted death. “If you’re selling a hot product, this is not it.” It’s not always clear what we’re trying to preserve: “I’m not even sure that I have a very good claim to be myself.” There’s an upside to life as a brain in a jar: “You can surf the internet
I do that pretty much 12 hours a day, anyway.” To find out which of these ideas might actually work, subscribers can now watch the full conversation on demand
Want to join the conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables
Read more: Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind Inside the stealthy startup that pitched brainless human clones Technology that lets us “speak” to our dead relatives has arrived

Are we ready? This researcher wants to replace your brain, little by little The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Trump has fired his cyber director after a wave of tech outages Pentagon official Kirsten Davies will replace Sean Cairncross. ( NBC News ) + The outages disrupted flights, banks and security systems. ( Reuters $) + They’ve fuelled fears of a wider collapse. ( WP $) + AI agents are expected to drive even more outages. A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive on life support outside the body for seven weeks, smashing the previous record of about two weeks
They achieved the feat by connecting a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste
The approach could open up new possibilities in biomedical engineering, from repairing damaged organs to growing new ones
Some researchers are even exploring artificial wombs

Take a closer look at the technology keeping human organs alive . —Antonio Regalado What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market After a tough few years littered with high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US: Sila has signed a deal with battery maker Panasonic Energy to supply silicon-carbon anode material that could be worth more than $1 billion
The agreement will help Sila scale production, potentially bringing smaller, lighter batteries to market
But it also reveals how battery politics have shifted
The factory is backed by a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department—and the industry is increasingly focused on geopolitics rather than the energy transition
